words.origin: Borrowed from Anglo-French *abeyaunce* "absence of a claimant or owner, lapse in succession," from *abaer, abair* "to open wide" (from *a-*, prefix in transitive verbs—from Latin *ad-* ad- — + *baer, baier* "to have the mouth wide open, gape, pant," from Vulgar Latin **batāre*, perhaps of imitative origin) + *-ance* -ance. First known use: circa 1530.
examples: … new contracts on all but one existing mine … are **in abeyance** pending the outcome of a government inquiry to be carried out into Australia's role in the nuclear fuel cycle. — Vimala Sarma
A plan that is currently being held **in abeyance**

words.definition: To solemnly renounce a belief or claim
words.origin: Middle English *abjuren*, borrowed from Anglo-French & Medieval Latin; Anglo-French *abjurer*, borrowed from Medieval Latin *abjūrāre*, "to repudiate, renounce (a right or claim), swear to stay away from," going back to Latin, "to deny knowledge of falsely under oath, repudiate," from *ab-* ab- + *jūrāre* "to swear". First known use: 15th century.
examples: He **abjured** his allegiance to his former country.

words.definition: The denial or giving up of one's own interests
words.origin: Middle English *abnegacioun*, borrowed from Late Latin *abnegātiōn-, abnegātiō*, from Latin *abnegāre* "to refute, decline, deny" + *-tiōn-, -tiō*, suffix of action nouns. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Monks practice **abnegation** of the material aspects of human life.
… Rennie Stennett, the Giants' $600,000-a-year bust of a second baseman, had, in a rush of **abnegation**, given away his money and was living on the beach, subsisting on abalone.

words.definition: To repeal or do away with a law or agreement
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *abrogātus*, past participle of *abrogāre*, "to repeal (a law), repudiate, cancel," from *ab-* ab- + *rogāre* "to ask, ask an assembly for approval of". First known use: circa 1520.
examples: The company's directors are accused of **abrogating** their responsibilities.

Continued progress in measurement and characterization of antibodies and strategies to **abrogate** antibody production both prior to and following heart transplant have been encouraging. — Peter M Eckman

words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *abstēmius* "refraining from wine, careful with one's means," from *abs-* (variant of *ab-* ab- before *c-* and *t-*) + *-tēmius*, from a base *tēm-* "intoxicating" (also in *tēmētum* "intoxicating beverage," *tēmulentus* "drunken"); if going back to an Indo-European root **temH-*, akin to Sanskrit *tāmyati* "(he/she) is stunned, loses consciousness, is exhausted," *tamayati* "(he/she) chokes (someone)," Armenian *tʿmrim* "(he/she) is stunned" (perhaps going back to **tēmiro-*). First known use: 1609.

Borrowed from Latin *abstrūsus* "concealed, recondite," from past participle of *abstrūdere* "to conceal," from *abs-* (variant of *ab-* ab- before *c-* and *t-*) + *trūdere* "to push, thrust". First known use: circa 1549.

words.definition: Gradual growth by the addition of layers
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *accrētiōn-, accrētiō* "increase," from *accrē-* (stem of *accrēscere* "to increase, be added") + *-tiōn-, -tiō*, suffix of action nouns. First known use: 1615.
Acerb + -ic. First known use: 1865.

Borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *acrimonie,* borrowed from Latin *ācrimōnia,* from *ācr-, ācer* "sharp, biting, keen" + *-mōnia,* suffix of abstract nouns (going back to the Indo-European noun-forming suffix **-mĕ̄n-/*-mŏ̄n-* + the abstract noun formative **-i-*). First known use: 1542.

words.definition: Clever and skilful, especially with the hands or mind
words.origin: Borrowed from French, going back to Old French, "handsome, elegant, skilled (in combat)," from *a-,* prefix, perhaps with intensive value (going back to Latin *ad-* ad-) + *droit* "straight, direct, true, regular," going back to Latin *directus* "straight, direct". First known use: 1652.

Borrowed from Latin *adumbrātus,* past participle of *adumbrāre* "to shade, represent by means of light and shade, sketch, outline," from *ad-* ad- + *-umbrāre,* verbal derivative of *umbra* "shadow". First known use: 1537.
examples: The social unrest that **adumbrated** the French Revolution
Bubbling optimism, not at all **adumbrated** by difficulties

words.origin: Borrowed from Latin, borrowed from Greek *aigís* "goatskin, mantle of Zeus," derivative of *aig-, aíx* "goat"; akin to Armenian *aic* "goat" (perhaps going back to Indo-European **h2eiǵ-ih2-*), and perhaps to Avestan *izaēna* "of leather". First known use: 15th century.
examples: Passed new laws under the **aegis** of national security

words.definition: Friendly and easy to talk to
words.origin: Middle English *affabyl,* borrowed from Anglo-French *affable,* borrowed from Latin *affābilis,* from *affārī* "to speak to, address" (from *ad-* ad- + *fārī* "to speak") + *-bilis* "capable of (being acted upon)". First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To make greater in power, rank or reputation
words.origin: Borrowed (with assimilation of the ending to -ize) from French *agrandiss-,* stem of *agrandir,* going back to Old French, from *a-,* verb-forming prefix (going back to Latin *ad-* ad-) + *-grandir,* verbal derivative of *grand* "large, great," going back to Latin *grandis* "fully grown, large, great". First known use: 1634.
Latin *alacritas*, from *alacr-, alacer* lively, eager. First known use: 15th century.
Alteration (after French *améliorer*) of meliorate. First known use: 1653.

words.definition: Without a clear shape or form
words.origin: Greek *amorphos*, from *a-* + *morphē* form. First known use: circa 1727.

words.definition: Something out of its proper time
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *anachronismus,* borrowed from Middle Greek *anachronismós,* from Late Greek *anachronízein* “to be late, (middle voice) be an anachronism” (from Greek *ana-* ana- + *chrónos* “time” + *-izein* -ize) + Greek *-ismos* -ism. First known use: 1617.
examples: I think the concept of the draft is an **anachronism** from the time before laptops and word processing software. — Sarah Manguso

words.origin: Late Latin *anathemat-, anathema*, from Greek, thing devoted to evil, curse, from *anatithenai* to set up, dedicate, from *ana-* + *tithenai* to place, set. First known use: 1582.
examples: Slashing tech work forces would have **been anathema** in Silicon Valley just a few years ago. — Mike Isaac
… this notion **was anathema to** most of his countrymen. — Stephen Jay Gould

words.origin: From *ancilla* + *-ry*. *Ancilla*: Latin, female servant. First known use: 1663.
examples: The main factory and its **ancillary** plants
… backers [of a proposed park] see all kinds of **ancillary** benefits, from health to traffic. — Lisa W. Foderaro

words.origin: Latin, spirit, mind, courage, anger. First known use: 1795.
examples: … the sixties mentality, with its strong **animus** against what it defines as "elitism" … — Daniel J. Singal

words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *antedīluviānus,* from Latin *ante-* ante- + *dīluvium* "flood, inundation" + *-ānus* -an. First known use: 1646.
examples: That **antediluvian** relic known as a slide rule

words.origin: Latin *antipathia*, from Greek *antipatheia*, from *antipathēs* of opposite feelings, from *anti-* + *pathos* experience. First known use: 1592.
examples: … perhaps his greatest **antipathies** were cabs, old women, doors that would not shut … — Charles Dickens

words.definition: A short, pithy statement of a truth
words.origin: Middle French *aphorisme*, from Late Latin *aphorismus*, from Greek *aphorismos* definition, aphorism, from *aphorizein* to define, from *apo-* + *horizein* to bound. First known use: 1528.
examples: The high-minded **aphorism**, "Let us value the quality of life, not the quantity"
These are dazzling chapters, packed with perfectly chosen anecdotes and pithy with **aphorism**. — John Keegan

words.definition: Of doubtful authenticity, though widely repeated
words.origin: Apocrypha + -al. First known use: 1553.
French *apogée*, from New Latin *apogaeum*, from Greek *apogaion*, from neuter of *apogeios, apogaios* far from the earth, from *apo-* + *gē, gaia* earth. First known use: 1640.
examples: Aegean civilization reached its **apogee** in Crete.

words.definition: The abandonment of a belief or cause
words.origin: Middle English *apostasie,* borrowed from Anglo-French, borrowed from Late Latin *apostasia,* borrowed from Greek *apostasía* "defection, revolt, (Septuagint) rebellion against God" (Late Greek, "defection, apostasy"), variant (with *-ia* -ia) of *apóstasis,* from *aposta-,* variant stem of *aphístamai, aphístasthai* "to stand away from, keep aloof from, revolt," middle voice of *aphístēmi, aphistánai* "to put away, remove, cause to revolt" (from *aph-,* assimilated variant of *apo-* apo- + *histánai* "to cause to stand, place") + *-sis* -sis. First known use: 14th century.

Borrowed from Latin *appositus* "situated near, ready at hand, suitable, apt," from past participle of *appōnere* "to place near, put or fit on, contribute as an additional element," from *ap-* ap-:1 + *pōnere* "to place, set, put in position". First known use: 1621.
From *approbate* + *-ion*. *Approbate*: Middle English, from Latin *approbatus*, past participle of *approbare*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: A plan that has won the **approbation** of the mayor

words.definition: The warmth of the sun on a winter's day
words.origin: From Latin *aprīcitās* "sunniness," from *aprīcus* "sunny". First known use: 1623.
Borrowed from Latin *arcānus* "secret, private, intimate," from *arca* "chest, coffer, box" + *-ānus* -an. First known use: 1547.

Middle English *ardaunt, ardent* "burning, fiery, passionate," borrowed from Middle French *ardent, ardant,* going back to Old French, borrowed from Latin *ardent-, ardens* "burning, fiercely hot, shining, eager, passionate," from present participle of *ardēre* "to burn, emit light or flame, be fiercely hot, be violently excited, be eager," derivative of *āridus, ārdus* "dry, waterless". First known use: 14th century.
Latin *arduus* high, steep, difficult; akin to Old Irish *ard* high. First known use: 1549.
examples: … a life of **arduous** toil. — A. C. Cole

words.origin: Borrowed from Anglo-French & Middle French, "trade, craft, craftsmanship, contrivance," borrowed from Latin *artificium* "artistry, craftsmanship, craft, craftiness, cunning," from *artific-, artifex* "practitioner of an art, specialist, craftsman, creator" (from *art-, ars* "acquired skill, craftsmanship" + *-fic-, -fex,* agentive derivative of *facere* "to make, bring about, do") + *-ium,* denominal or deverbal suffix of function or state. First known use: 1540.
examples: … believing that characters had to be created from within rather than with **artifice**. — Garson Kanin
… revising the state's constitution through a series of legal stratagems and **artifices** … — W. Haywood Burns

words.origin: Greek *askētikos*, literally, laborious, from *askētēs* one that exercises, hermit, from *askein* to work, exercise. First known use: 1646.
Latin *assiduus*, from *assidēre* to sit beside. First known use: circa 1552.
examples: She tended her garden with **assiduous** attention.

words.definition: To ease or soothe a feeling
words.origin: Middle English *aswagen,* borrowed from Anglo-French *asuager* (continental Old French *assuagier*), going back to Vulgar Latin **assūaviāre,* from Latin *ad-* -ad- + Vulgar Latin **-sūaviāre,* derivative of Latin *sūavis* "agreeable to the senses, sweet, pleasant". First known use: 14th century.
examples: No explanation or rationale could **assuage** our shock, pain and grief. — Ian T. Douglas

words.definition: Reverting to something ancestral or primitive
words.origin: French *atavisme*, from Latin *atavus* ancestor, from *at-* (probably akin to *atta* daddy) + *avus* grandfather. First known use: 1833.

words.definition: To weaken or reduce in force
examples: … shows great skill in the use of language to moderate or **attenuate** the impact of awkward facts. — Bernard Lewis

words.definition: Showing bold, daring disregard for risk
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French *audacieux,* from *audace* "daring, recklessness" (borrowed from Latin *audācia,* from *audāc-, audāx* "daring, bold, excessively daring, reckless" + *-ia* -ia) + *-ieux* -ious; *audāx* from *audēre* "to intend, dare, venture" (verbal derivative of *avidus* "ardent, eager, greedy") + *-āc-, -āx,* deverbal suffix denoting habitual or successful performance (probably going back to Indo-European **-eh2,* noun ending + **-k-,* suffixal formative). First known use: 1550.

words.definition: To portend a good or bad outcome
words.origin: Middle English *augurre, augure,* borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *augure,* borrowed from Latin *augur,* perhaps going back to **aug-u-s* "the increased, one who receives the signs of increase," noun derivative of an s-stem adjective **aug-u-s* "increased, grown," derivative of a u-stem adjective **aug-u-* with the same sense, derivative from the base of *augeō, augēre* "to increase, make greater, heighten". First known use: 14th century.
Latin *auspicium* auspice + -ous. First known use: 1593.
examples: … a festival that takes place during the hottest months of spring, just before the monsoon rains, and that is considered an **auspicious** time for weddings. — Cynthia Gorney

In days of old, seers entered a trance state and then informed anxious seekers what kind of mood the gods were in, and whether this was an **auspicious** time to begin a journey, get married, or start a war. — Harvey Cox

words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *austerus*, from Greek *austēros* harsh, severe; akin to Greek *hauos* dry. First known use: 14th century.
examples: An **austere**… figure too remote for love from his children. — Eileen Lockwood
**… austere** critics who decry sentimentality … — Fisun Güner

words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *avaritia*, from *avarus* avaricious, from *avēre* to crave. First known use: 13th century.
examples: … an era of nearly unbridled **avarice** on Wall Street … — Matthew Campbell and Kit Chellel

words.definition: Kind and friendly, like an uncle
words.origin: Latin *avunculus* maternal uncle. First known use: 1831.
examples: Jovial and **avuncular**, the President's chief of staff seems oblivious to the pressures that accompany what is arguably the second most powerful job in the land. — Craig Unger
Two weeks of poker had led to his writing to his uncle a distressed, but confident, request for more funds; and the **avuncular** foot had come down with a joyous bang. — P. G. Wodehouse

words.origin: Borrowed from French, going back to Middle French, "foolishness, stupidity," from *badiner* "to banter, jest, play the fool" (verbal derivative of *badin* "silly, foolish," as noun, "fool, simpleton," borrowed from Occitan, from *badar* "to have the mouth wide open, gape"—going back to Vulgar Latin **batāre*, perhaps of imitative origin + *-in*, adjective suffix) + *-age* -age. First known use: circa 1658.

Middle English *balefull* "(of humans or animals) bent upon mischief or destruction, malevolent, (of things) pernicious," also "wretched, miserable," going back to Old English *bealluful* "full of evil, sinful," from *bealu* bale + *-ful* -ful. First known use: before 12th century.

Borrowed from French, "pertaining to a feudal lord's right to extract usage fees for mills, ovens, etc., within his jurisdiction, available for general use, ordinary, commonplace, trite," going back to Old French *bannel* "subject to a feudal lord's jurisdiction, of seigneurial authority," borrowed from Medieval Latin *bannālis, banālis* "ordered by a ban, invested with public authority," from *bannus, bannum* "order given by a public authority, authority, jurisdiction" (borrowed from Old Low Franconian **banna-* "call to arms by a lord") + Latin *-ālis* -al. First known use: 1825.
examples: The writing was **banal**, but the story was good.
We've all gotten mired in **banal** small talk at some point. — Sue Shellenbarger

words.definition: An abrupt, ludicrous drop from the lofty to the trivial
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *báthos* "depth," neuter s-stem derivative of *bathýs* "deep". First known use: 1727.

words.definition: To charm, often in a deceptive way
words.origin: Middle English *bigilen, beguilen*, from *bi-, be-* be- + *gile* guile or *gilen* "to deceive, cheat," borrowed from Old French *guiler*, derivative of *guile*. First known use: 13th century.
examples: **Beguiled** her classmates into doing the work for her

words.definition: To give a false impression of
words.origin: Middle English *belien*, going back to Old English *belēogan*, from *be-* be- + *lēogan* "to lie". First known use: before 12th century.
examples: His manner and appearance **belie** his age.

words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *bellicosus*, from *bellicus* of war, from *bellum* war. First known use: 15th century.

examples: **Benighted** travellers … have seen his midnight candle glimmering. — W. B. Yeats
Spreading their message among these poor **benighted** people

words.definition: Deprived of something; lonely and abandoned
examples: Both players are instantly **bereft** of their poise … — A. E. Wier
… the book is … completely **bereft** of an index.

words.origin: Middle French *bilieux*, from Latin *biliosus*, from *bilis*. First known use: 1541.
examples: With clapboards painted red and **bilious** yellow — Sinclair Lewis

words.origin: Blandish + -ment, probably after Anglo-French *blandisement, blaundissement* and continental Old & Middle French *blandissement*. First known use: circa 1553.
examples: … refuses to yield to their **blandishments** … — Irving Babbitt

words.definition: Cheerfully carefree, sometimes too much so
words.origin: Middle English, from Old English *blīthe*; akin to Old High German *blīdi* joyous. First known use: before 12th century.
examples: A **blithe** disregard for the rights of others

words.origin: Earlier, "cotton or other material used as padding or stuffing," extension (with parasitic *t*) of *bombace, bombage,* going back to Middle English *bombace,* borrowed from Anglo-French *bombés, bombace,* borrowed from Medieval Latin *bambac-, bambax, bombax* (also *banbax, bonbax*) "cotton plant, cotton fibre or wadding," borrowed from Middle Greek *bámbax, pámbax,* going back to a Greek stem *pambak-* (as in *pambakís* "item of clothing, probably of cotton"), probably borrowed from Middle Persian *pambak* "cotton" (or from an unknown source from which both words were borrowed). First known use: 1577.
French *bonhomie*, from *bonhomme* good-natured man, from *bon* good + *homme* man. First known use: 1777.
examples: … exuded an aura of cheerful **bonhomie**. — Alistair MacLean

words.origin: From *boor* + *-ish*. *Boor*: Dutch *boer*; akin to Old English *būan* to dwell. First known use: 1562.

words.definition: To remove material considered improper from a text
words.origin: Thomas *Bowdler* †1825 English editor. First known use: 1826.

words.definition: Abrupt or offhand in speech or manner
words.origin: Borrowed from French, borrowed from Italian *brusco* "(of a person's manner) rough, rude, abrupt," also "(of wine, food) sharp, pungent," going back to a pre-Latin expressive base **brūsk-,* denoting prickliness, roughness. First known use: circa 1639.

words.definition: Relating to the pleasant aspects of country life
words.origin: Latin *bucolicus*, from Greek *boukolikos*, from *boukolos* cowherd, from *bous* head of cattle + *-kolos* (akin to Latin *colere* to cultivate). First known use: circa 1609.
Bump + *-tious* (as in *fractious*). First known use: 1801.
Middle English *burjonen*, from Anglo-French *burjuner*, from *burjun* bud, from Vulgar Latin **burrion-, burrio*, from Late Latin *burra* fluff, shaggy cloth. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … when the flame trees and jacaranda are **burgeoning** … — Alan Carmichael
The market has **burgeoned** in recent years.

words.origin: French *cabale* cabala, intrigue, cabal, from Medieval Latin *cabbala* cabala, from Late Hebrew *qabbālāh*, literally, received (lore). First known use: 1614.

words.definition: A harsh, discordant mixture of sounds
words.origin: Borrowed from French & New Latin; French *cacophonie,* going back to Middle French, borrowed from New Latin *cacophōnia,* borrowed from Greek *kakophōnía,* from *kakóphōnos* "disagreeable-sounding, cacophonous" + *-ia* -ia. First known use: circa 1656.

words.definition: The rise and fall of a voice or rhythm
words.origin: Middle English, “rhythm of prose or verse, rhetorical periods,” borrowed from Medieval Latin *cadentia* “rhythm in verse,” noun derivative (formally feminine singular from neuter plural) of Latin *cadent-, cadens,* present participle of *cadere* “to fall, sound rhythmically, end, terminate (of words or clauses)”. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To persuade by flattery or coaxing
words.origin: Borrowed from French *cajoler* "to give much attention to, make a fuss over, flatter, persuade with flattery," going back to Middle French *cajoller* "to flatter out of self-interest," perhaps the same verb as Middle French *cageoller* "to vocalize, sing (of a jay or other bird)," expressive formation of uncertain origin. First known use: 1630.
Middle English *calu* bald, from Old English; akin to Old High German *kalo* bald, Old Church Slavic *golŭ* bare. First known use: 1580.

words.definition: A false statement made to damage someone's reputation
words.origin: Middle English *calumnye*, from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *calomnie*, from Latin *calumnia*, from *calvi* to deceive; perhaps akin to Old English *hōlian* to slander, Greek *kēlein* to beguile. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Denounced his opponent for his defamatory insinuations and **calumny**
He was the target of **calumny** for his unpopular beliefs.

words.origin: French, literally, duck; in sense 1, from Middle French *vendre des canards à moitié* to cheat, literally, to half-sell ducks. First known use: 1843.
examples: The report about a conspiracy proved to be a **canard**.
The widespread **canard** that every lawyer is dishonest

words.origin: Borrowed from French & Latin; French *candeur,* borrowed from Latin *candōr-, candor* "brightness, radiance, whiteness, disposition to think well (of)," noun derivative in *-ōr-* corresponding to *candēre* "to shine, be white," *candidus* "bright, white". First known use: 14th century.
examples: … a rare moment of **candour** from a master of obfuscation … — Anthony Faiola

words.definition: Given to sudden changes of mood or behaviour
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French *capricieux,* borrowed from Italian *capriccioso,* from *capriccio* caprice + *-oso* -ous. First known use: 1588.
examples: … the belief … that we were mere pieces in the games of **capricious** gods. — Diane Weber Bederman
The **capricious** nature of the stock market

words.definition: Inclined to find fault over trifles
words.origin: Middle English *capcious*, from Middle French or Latin; Middle French *captieux*, from Latin *captiosus*, from *captio* deception, verbal quibble, from *capere* to take. First known use: 14th century.
French, from Spanish *carapacho*. First known use: 1836.
examples: The **carapace** of reserve he built around himself … — M. M. Mintz

words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *castīgātus,* past participle of *castīgāre* "to discipline for a fault or lapse, reprove, censure," perhaps from **casti-,* stem of **castis* "reprimand" (going back to Indo-European **ḱHs-ti-,* whence also Sanskrit *śiṣṭi-* "instruction") + **-ig-,* going back to Indo-European *-h2ǵ-,* zero-grade of **h2eǵ-* "drive, impel, lead". First known use: 1606.
examples: The judge **castigated** the lawyers for their lack of preparation.

words.definition: Release of strong emotion, bringing relief
words.origin: New Latin, from Greek *katharsis*, from *kathairein* to cleanse, purge, from *katharos*. First known use: circa 1775.
Latin *causticus*, from Greek *kaustikos*, from *kaiein* to burn. First known use: 14th century.
examples: The chemical was so **caustic** that it ate through the pipe.

words.origin: Latin *cavillari* to jest, cavil, from *cavilla* raillery; akin to Latin *calvi* to deceive. First known use: 1542.
examples: The author **caviled** about the design of the book's cover.
He **caviled** the conditions of the agreement.

words.origin: Middle English *celerite*, borrowed from Anglo-French *celeritee*, borrowed from Latin *celeritāt-, celeritās* from *celer* "swift, speedy" + *-itāt-, -itās* -ity. First known use: 15th century.
examples: **Celerity** of movement is vital in war.

words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *censure*, borrowed from Latin *cēnsūa* "office of censor, assessment, moral oversight," from *cēnsēre* "to give as an opinion, perform the duties of a censor" + *-ūra* -ure. First known use: 1539.
examples: Unorthodox practices awaiting the **censure** of the city council
The country faces international **censure** for its alleged involvement in the assassination.

words.definition: Annoyance at having failed or been humiliated
words.origin: French, from *chagrin* sad. First known use: 1661.

Borrowed from French *chicanerie* "quibbling on minor points of law brought up to complicate a judicial case," going back to Middle French *chiquanerie,* from *chicaner* "to dispute by means of quibbles," earlier "to sue, prosecute" + *-erie* -ery. First known use: 1589.
examples: He wasn't above using **chicanery** to win votes.

words.definition: An illusion or fanciful hope that can never be realized
words.origin: Latin *chimaera*, from Greek *chimaira* she-goat, chimera; akin to Old Norse *gymbr* yearling ewe, Greek *cheimōn* winter. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … a fancy, a **chimera** in my brain, troubles me in my prayer. — John Donne

words.origin: Middle English *colerik* "of the humour bile, having excess bile," borrowed from Anglo-French *colerique,* borrowed from Late Latin *colericus, cholericus* "bilious," borrowed from Greek *cholerikós* "of cholera," from *choléra* cholera + *-ikos*. First known use: 1556.

Middle English *cherlyssh* "of churls, rustic, uncouth," going back to Old English *ceorlisc, cyrlisc,* from *ceorl* "male person, countryman, member of the lowest class of free men" + *-isc* -ish. First known use: before 12th century.
examples: He didn't like the **churlish** tone in his voice. — Margaret Truman
Outrage is among your more **churlish** emotions — Robert Goldsborough

words.definition: Using many words where few would do
words.origin: Middle English *circumlocucyon*, from Latin *circumlocution-, circumlocutio*, from *circum-* + *locutio* speech, from *loqui* to speak. First known use: circa 1518.

words.definition: A loud and confused noise, especially of protest
words.origin: Middle English *clamour,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *clamur, clamour,* borrowed from Latin *clāmor,* from *clāmāre* "to shout, utter a loud cry" + *-or* -or. First known use: 14th century.
Middle French or Latin; Middle French *clandestin*, from Latin *clandestinus*, from *clam* secretly; akin to Latin *celare* to hide. First known use: circa 1528.

From *cloy* + *-ing*. *Cloy*: Middle English, to hinder, lame, alteration of *acloyen* to harm, maim, modification of Anglo-French *encloer* to nail, prick a horse with a nail in shoeing, from Medieval Latin *inclavare*, from Latin *in* + *clavus* nail. First known use: 1594.
examples: Her coyness grows **cloying** after a while … — Elysa Gardner

words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *cōgent-, cōgens,* present participle of *cōgere* "to drive together, gather, compress, force, compel," from *co-,* variant before a vowel and *h* of *com-* com- + *agere* "to drive (cattle), be in motion, do". First known use: 1659.
Cogniz(ance) + -ant. First known use: 1820.
examples: … they should have been a little more **cognizant** of what the airport's needs would be. — Tom Gougeon, quoted in *The Denver Post*

words.origin: Middle English *colloquie* "discourse," borrowed from Latin *colloquium* "talk, conversation, conference, discussion," from *colloquor, colloquī* "to talk, converse, discuss" (from *col-* col- + *loquī* "to talk, speak") + *-ium,* suffix of deverbal compounds. First known use: 15th century.
examples: A **colloquy** between the trial judge and defendant

words.definition: Courtesy and considerate behaviour toward others
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *cōmitāt-, cōmitās* "friendliness, courtesy, graciousness," from *cōmis* "kind, obliging, gracious" (probably going back to Old Latin *cosmis,* of uncertain origin) + *-itāt- -itās* -ity. First known use: 1543.

words.definition: In proportion to; corresponding in size or degree
words.origin: Late Latin *commensuratus*, from Latin *com-* + Late Latin *mensuratus*, past participle of *mensurare* to measure, from Latin *mensura* measure. First known use: 1641.
examples: Was given a job **commensurate** with her abilities
Lived a life **commensurate** with the early years of the republic

words.definition: A feeling of guilt that prevents wrongdoing
words.origin: Middle English *compunccioun*, from Anglo-French *compunction*, from Late Latin *compunction-, compunctio*, from Latin *compungere* to prick hard, sting, from *com-* + *pungere* to prick. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … showed no **compunction** in planning devilish engines of … destruction. — Havelock Ellis
… he had no **compunction** about brushing aside legal technicalities. — Robert Penn Warren

words.origin: Latin *concomitant-, concomitans*, present participle of *concomitari* to accompany, from *com-* + *comitari* to accompany, from *comit-, comes* companion. First known use: 1607.
Borrowed from Latin *conflagrātiōn-, conflagrātiō,* from *conflagrāre* "to be destroyed by fire, be burnt down" + *-tiōn-, -tiō,* suffix of verbal action. First known use: 1600.
examples: The **conflagration** between the two countries lasted for ten years.

words.definition: Pleasant because suited to one's tastes
words.origin: *com-* + *genius*. First known use: circa 1625.

words.definition: To secretly allow or conspire in wrongdoing
words.origin: French or Latin; French *conniver*, from Latin *conivēre, connivēre* to close the eyes, connive, from *com-* + *-nivēre* (akin to *nictare* to wink); akin to Old English & Old High German *hnīgan* to bow. First known use: 1601.
examples: The government **connived** in the rebels' military buildup.
The captain **connived** at the smuggling of goods aboard his ship.

words.definition: Anxiety or dismay, often at something unexpected
words.origin: French or Latin; French, from Latin *consternation-, consternatio*, from *consternare* to throw into confusion, from *com-* + *-sternare*, probably from *sternere* to spread, strike down. First known use: 1604.
examples: … the two … stared at each other in **consternation**, and neither knew what to do. — Pearl Buck

words.origin: Middle English *contrit,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Medieval Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Medieval Latin *contrītus,* past participle of Latin *conterere* "to pound to pieces, crush, wear out or down, exhaust mentally or physically" (Medieval Latin also, "to crush in spirit with a sense of one's sin, render contrite"), from *con-* con- + *terere* "to rub, grind, crush, wear down". First known use: 14th century.
examples: I have a sense now of his feeling somewhat **contrite**, or perhaps only abashed. — Renata Adler
Ford executives had hoped their efficient, well-publicized recall efforts and **contrite** approach to customers would enable them to put the tire crisis behind them. — Cathy Booth Thomas

words.origin: Middle English *contumelie*, from Middle French, from Latin *contumelia*. First known use: 14th century.
Late Latin *convivialis*, from Latin *convivium* banquet, from *com-* + *vivere* to live. First known use: circa 1668.
Middle English, from Latin *copiosus*, from *copia* abundance, from *co-* + *ops* wealth. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … Shakespeare, whose soul was so **copious** … — Gilbert Highet

words.origin: French, feminine of *coquet*. First known use: circa 1611.
examples: … the book brought to mind a true Southern **coquette**, flashy and sweet and alluring all at the same time. — Tina Jordan
… the rufous-crested **coquette**, a tiny hummingbird (with a red mohawk "hair-do") that was just as … flirty as its name. — Thelma Dalmas

words.origin: Middle English *correlary, corolarie,* borrowed from Late Latin *corōllārium,* going back to Latin, "garland (given as a reward), unsolicited payment, gratuity," from *corōlla* "small wreath of flowers" + *-ārium* -ary. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … love was a stormy passion and jealousy its normal **corollary**. — Ida Treat
A **corollary** to the problem of the number of vessels to be built was that of the types of vessels to be constructed. — Daniel Marx

words.definition: A small, exclusive group of people
words.origin: Borrowed from French, "group of persons joined by a common interest," earlier, "group of peasants owing labour service or rent to a lord," going back to Middle French (Picard) "tenure of a free peasant," from *cotier* "peasant on a smallholding, cottar" + *-erie* -ery. First known use: 1738.

Middle English *contenance*, from Anglo-French *cuntenance, contenance*, from Medieval Latin *continentia*, from Latin, restraint, from *continent-, continens*, present participle of *continēre* to hold together. First known use: 13th century.
examples: … a **countenance** which expressed both good humour and intelligence … — Sir Walter Scott
… startled, and also somewhat out of **countenance**. — Arnold Bennett

words.definition: To yearn to possess something belonging to another
words.origin: Middle English *coveiten*, from Anglo-French *coveiter*, from Vulgar Latin **cupidietare*, from Latin *cupiditat-, cupiditas* desire, from *cupidus* desirous, from *cupere* to desire. First known use: 14th century.
Latin *credulus*, from *credere* to believe, entrust. First known use: 1553.
examples: Few people are **credulous** enough to believe such nonsense.

words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *crepusculāris,* from Latin *crepusculum* "twilight" + *-āris* -ar. First known use: 1668.
Middle English *cupidite*, from Anglo-French *cupidité*, from Latin *cupiditat-, cupiditas*. First known use: 15th century.
Of uncertain origin. First known use: 1568.
examples: The film follows Otto, an older man who has become a **curmudgeon** upon the loss of his wife from cancer. — Adrianna Freedman
This is a story about a **curmudgeon** who is so disgruntled with life but starts to make connections with his new neighbours. — Abby Corson

words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *cursōrius* "of running, swift" (Late Latin in nominal derivatives, as *cursōria* "shoe for running"), adjectival derivative of Latin *cursor* "runner". First known use: 1601.
examples: Only a **cursory** inspection of the building's electrical wiring was done.

words.definition: A casual romantic or sexual relationship
words.origin: From *dally* + *-ance*. *Dally*: Middle English *dalyen*, from Anglo-French *dalier*. First known use: 14th century.
Middle English *derthe*, from Old English **dierth*, from *dēore* dear. First known use: 13th century.

French *débâcle*, from *débâcler* to clear, from Middle French *desbacler*, from *des-* de- + *bacler* to block, perhaps from Vulgar Latin **bacculare*, from Latin *baculum* staff. First known use: 1802.

Middle English *debonere, debonaire* "mild, meek, kind, courteous," borrowed from Anglo-French *deboneire, debonaire* "mild, meek, noble, highborn," from *de* "of" + *bon* "good" + Old French *aire, ere* "family, stock, sort, kind". First known use: 13th century.

Latin decōrus "good-looking, handsome, worthy of approval, suitable" (derivative of *decōr-, decor* "pleasing appearance, beauty, grace, seemliness, propriety," derivative from the stem of *decet, decēre* "to add grace to, adorn, be fitting or proper") + -ous. First known use: 1653.
examples: Ever **decorous**, she periodically excuses herself to another room rather than allow a guest to witness her blowing her nose. — Will Hermes

words.definition: To throw out of a window
words.origin: *de-* + Latin *fenestra* window. First known use: 1619.
Borrowed from French *déférence,* going back to Middle French *deference* "act of submitting," from *deferer* "to submit to another, defer" + *-ence* -ence. First known use: 1660.
Greek *dēlētērios*, from *dēleisthai* to hurt. First known use: 1587.

words.definition: A leader who exploits popular prejudice
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *dēmagōgós,* from *dêmos* "people" + *-agōgos* "leading, impelling". First known use: 1629.
examples: The most fervent devotees of a cult or **demagogue** are those who mistake courtship for love and the power of a leader for their own. — Greg Jackson

words.definition: To raise doubts or show reluctance
words.origin: Middle English *demuren, demeren* to linger, from Anglo-French *demurer, demoerer*, from Latin *demorari*, from *de-* + *morari* to linger, from *mora* delay. First known use: 13th century.
examples: It would seem hazardous to **demur** to a proposition which is so widely accepted. — Samuel Alexander

words.definition: The final resolution of a plot
words.origin: French *dénouement*, literally, untying, from Middle French *desnouement*, from *desnouer* to untie, from Old French *desnoer*, from *des-* de- + *noer* to tie, from Latin *nodare*, from *nodus* knot. First known use: 1705.
examples: In the novel's **denouement**, the two hostages escape to freedom.
It is an intentionally unsettling **denouement**, which is in keeping with the tone and purpose of the entire miniseries. — David Wiegand

words.origin: Latin *deprecatus*, past participle of *deprecari* to avert by prayer, from *de-* + *precari* to pray. First known use: 1628.
examples: … speaks five languages … but **deprecates** this facility …

words.origin: Latin *deridēre*, from *de-* + *ridēre* to laugh. First known use: circa 1526.
examples: … how they mock and **deride** him as he slinks away. — Charles Dickens
These artists were a plucky band of underdogs and the conventional art community found all kinds of ways to **deride** them. — Diane Urbani de la Paz

words.origin: Latin *desiccatus*, past participle of *desiccare* to dry up, from *de-* + *siccare* to dry, from *siccus* dry. First known use: 1575.
examples: … a charming little romance … not **desiccated** and compressed within the pages of a book … — Elinor Wylie
Lake Valencia has been … steadily **desiccating** for more than 200 years. — J. Platt Bradbury et al.

words.definition: Lacking a plan or purpose; half-hearted
words.origin: Latin *desultorius*, literally, of a circus rider who leaps from horse to horse, from *desilire* to leap down, from *de-* + *salire* to leap. First known use: 1581.
examples: … a dragged-out ordeal of … **desultory** shopping. — Herman Wouk

words.origin: Extension with -ous of Medieval Latin *diafanus, diaphanus,* borrowed from Greek *diaphanḗs* "transparent, manifest, conspicuous," adjective derivative from the stem of *diaphaínein* "to let be seen through," *diaphaínesthai* "to show through, be seen through," from *dia-* dia- + *phaínein* (active voice) "to bring to light, cause to appear," and *phaínesthai* (middle voice) "to become visible, come to light, appear". First known use: 1614.
examples: Had only a **diaphanous** hope of success

words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin, "disputation," going back to Latin, "school (of rhetoric or philosophy)," borrowed from Greek *diatribḗ* "wearing down, attrition, spending of time, discussion, discourse, school," derivative of *diatrī́bein* "to crush, wear out, spend time, occupy oneself," from *dia-* dia- + *trī́bein* "to rub, grind, wear down," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1581.

Borrowed from New Latin *didacticus,* borrowed from Greek *didaktikós* "apt at teaching," from *didaktós* "taught, learned" (verbal adjective of *didáskein*, aorist *edídaxa* "to teach, instruct," factitive derivative of *daênai* "to learn") + *-ikos* -ic; *daênai* going back to Indo-European **dens-, *dn̥s-* "become knowledgeable or skillful," whence also Avestan *dīdaiŋ́hē* "(I) learn, experience" and, in nominal derivatives, Sanskrit *dáṃsaḥ* "marvelous power," *dasráḥ* "accomplishing wonderful deeds," and perhaps Greek *dḗnea* "plans, intentions". First known use: 1658.
examples: The first part of the book is more **didactic**, with lengthy descriptions of how the operating system actually works. — Richard C. Leinecker
The best of her poems are brilliant and compelling; others are uneven and feel talky or **didactic**. — Elizabeth Lund

words.definition: Modest or shy from a lack of confidence
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Latin *diffīdent-, diffīdens* "distrustful, lacking in confidence," from present participle of *diffīdere* "to lack confidence (in), have no trust (in)," from *dif-,* assimilated form of *dis-* dis- + *fīdere* "to trust, have confidence (in)," going back to Indo-European **bhei̯dh-* "trust, entrust". First known use: 15th century.
Middle English, from Anglo-French *dilatorie*, Late Latin *dilatorius*, from Latin *differre* (past participle *dilatus*) to postpone, differ. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A dabbler in the arts without real commitment
words.origin: Borrowed from Italian, agentive derivative of *dilettare* "to please, delight," borrowed from Latin *dēlectāre*. First known use: 1748.
examples: Mr. Carroll often criticizes the superficial lives of the **dilettantes** … who mingle in New York. — Mark Stevens
Whitman ran an amateurish campaign … and was painted as an aristocratic **dilettante**. — Eleanor Clift

words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *descumfit*, past participle of *descumfire*, from *des-* dis- + *cumfire* to prepare. First known use: 13th century.
examples: … was **discomfited** in a great battle … — Edward Gibbon

words.origin: Middle English, from Medieval Latin *disconsolatus*, from Latin *dis-* + *consolatus*, past participle of *consolari* to console. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … a clutch of **disconsolate** houses. — D. H. Lawrence
The team returned **disconsolate** from three losses

words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *discursīvus* "showing reasoned thought, logical," from *discursus,* past participle of *discurrere* "to range over, discuss" (going back to Latin, "to run off in different directions, [of a mind or speaker] branch out, range") + Latin *-īvus* -ive. First known use: 1595.

Borrowed from Latin *disparātus* "separate, distinct," from past participle of *disparāre* "to divide, separate off, make different," from *dis-* dis- + *parāre* "to supply, provide, make ready" (influenced in sense by association with *dispar-, dispār* "unequal, different"). First known use: 1566.
examples: Its **disparate** parts don't quite jell, and the ending feels rushed. — Don Aucoin

words.definition: To conceal one's true motives or feelings
words.origin: Middle English *dissymbulen, dissymblen,* probably reshaping of *dissimulen* in same sense (after *resemblen* "to resemble," *semblance* semblance, and like forms), borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *dissimuler, dissumuler* "to hide under a false appearance," borrowed from Latin *dissimulāre*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: He had **dissembled** about the risks involved.

words.definition: Lax in morals; given to vice
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *dissolutus*, from past participle of *dissolvere* to loosen, dissolve. First known use: 14th century.
examples: The **dissolute** and degrading aspects of human nature — Wallace Fowlie

words.origin: From *dissonant*. *Dissonant*: Middle English *dissonaunte*, from Latin *dissonant-, dissonans*, present participle of *dissonare* to be discordant, from *dis-* + *sonare* to sound. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The **dissonance** between the truth and what people want to believe
The mingling of bitter comedy and stark tragedy produces sharp **dissonances** … — F. B. Millett

words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *diurnalis*. First known use: 14th century.
Middle English *dogerel*, probably diminutive of *dogge* dog. First known use: 15th century.
From *dogma* + *-tic*. *Dogma*: Latin *dogmat-, dogma*, from Greek, from *dokein* to seem. First known use: 1681.
From *dolor* + *-ous*. *Dolor*: Middle English *dolour*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *dolor* pain, grief, from *dolēre* to feel pain, grieve. First known use: 15th century.
Middle English, from Latin *durus* hard. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … an insistent hunger for learning and a **dour** … determination to achieve it. — Walter Moberly

words.origin: Latin *Dracon-, Draco*, from Greek *Drakōn* Draco (Athenian lawgiver). First known use: 1752.

words.definition: Sweet and soothing to the ear
words.origin: Middle English *doucet*, from Anglo-French, from *duz, douz* sweet, from Latin *dulcis*; perhaps akin to Greek *glykys* sweet. First known use: 15th century.
Middle English *duplicite*, from Middle French, from Late Latin *duplicitat-, duplicitas*, from Latin *duplex*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … the simplicity and openness of their lives brought out for him the **duplicity** that lay at the bottom of ours. — Mary Austin

words.origin: Latin *ebullient-, ebulliens*, present participle of *ebullire* to bubble out, from *e-* + *bullire* to bubble, boil. First known use: 1599.

words.definition: Drawing on a wide range of sources
words.origin: Borrowed from Greek *eklektikós* "picking out, selecting what appears to be best," from *eklektós* "picked out, select" (verbal adjective of *eklégein* "to pick out, select," from *ek-* ec- + *légein* "to collect, gather, count, say") + *-ikos* -ic. First known use: 1683.

words.definition: To instruct or improve morally or intellectually
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *edifier*, from Late Latin & Latin; Late Latin *aedificare* to instruct or improve spiritually, from Latin, to erect a house, from *aedes* temple, house; akin to Old English *ād* funeral pyre, Latin *aestas* summer. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To erase; to make oneself inconspicuous
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *esfacer, effacer*, from *e-* + *face* face. First known use: 15th century.

examples: She was a marvel with the press: fresh, direct, **effervescent**. — Bruce Anderson

words.origin: Latin *effetus*, from *ex-* + *fetus* fruitful. First known use: 1660.
examples: … the **effete** monarchies … of feudal Europe … — G. M. Trevelyan
… macrophages that recycle used iron from **effete** red cells. — Nancy C. Andrews

words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French *efficace* "effective" or its source Latin *efficāc-, efficāx* "capable of fulfilling a function, effective" (from *efficere* "to make, bring about, produce, carry out" + *-āc-, -āx,* deverbal suffix denoting habitual or successful performance) + -ious. First known use: 1528.
French *effronterie*, ultimately from Medieval Latin *effront-, effrons* shameless, from Latin *ex-* + *front-, frons* forehead. First known use: 1641.

Borrowed from Late Latin *effulgentia* "radiance," noun derivative of Latin *effulgent-, effulgens,* present participle of *effulgēre* "to shine or blaze forth, flash," from *ef-,* variant before *f* of *ex-* ex-:1 + *fulgēre* "to shine brightly, flash, lighten". First known use: 1667.
Latin *egregius*, from *e-* + *greg-, grex* herd. First known use: circa 1550.
examples: Is there one lie that seems to be the most repeated or, in your view, is the most **egregious**? — Meredith Blake
**Egregious** padding of the evidence — Christopher Hitchens

words.origin: Perhaps from Middle English **elfriche* fairyland, from Middle English *elf* + *riche* kingdom, from Old English *rīce*. First known use: 1508.
examples: And the woman, whose voice had risen to a kind of **eldritch** singsong, turned with a skip, and was gone. — Robert Louis Stevenson
… the film works its whimsically **eldritch** spell through inspired casting, brilliant editing, and subtly astonishing special effects … — Ty Burr

words.definition: A mournful poem, often for the dead
words.origin: Latin *elegia* poem in elegiac couplets, from Greek *elegeia, elegeion*, from *elegos* song of mourning. First known use: 1501.

Borrowed from Late Latin *ēlūcidātus,* past participle of *ēlūcidāre* "to enlighten, explain," from Latin *ē-,* variant of *ex-* ex-:1 + *-lūcidāre,* derivative of *lūcidus* "bright, shining, clear to the understanding". First known use: circa 1568.
Latin *emollient-, emolliens*, present participle of *emollire* to soften, from *e-* + *mollis* soft. First known use: 1612.
examples: … soothe us in our agonies with **emollient** words … — H. L. Mencken

words.definition: A speech or text in high praise
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *enkōmion*, from *en* in + *kōmos* revel, celebration. First known use: 1567.

words.definition: To drain of energy or vitality
words.origin: Latin *enervatus*, past participle of *enervare*, from *e-* + *nervus* sinew. First known use: 1605.

words.definition: To cause or give rise to
words.origin: Middle English *engendren*, from Anglo-French *engendrer*, from Latin *ingenerare*, from *in-* + *generare* to generate. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Listless weariness from lack of interest
words.origin: French, from Old French *enui* annoyance, from *enuier* to vex, from Late Latin *inodiare* to make loathsome. First known use: 1732.
examples: Suffered from a general sense of **ennui**
… chronicling the existential **ennui** of modern life … — Eli Glasner

words.origin: Greek *ephēmeros* lasting a day, daily, from *epi-* + *hēmera* day. First known use: 1576.
examples: Their fame turned out to be **ephemeral**.
… the **ephemeral** nature of journalism … — Evelyn Toynton

words.definition: A person devoted to refined food and drink
words.origin: *Epicurus*. First known use: 1551.

Middle English *epigrame,* borrowed from Latin *epigrammat-, epigramma* "inscription, epitaph, epigram," borrowed from Greek *epigrammat-, epígramma* "inscription on a tomb, monument or work of art" (Late Greek, "short poem, epigram"), from *epigráphein* "to mark the surface of, graze, scratch a mark on, inscribe" (from *epi-* epi- + *gráphein* "to cut into, scratch, inscribe, write") + *-mat-, -ma,* resultative noun suffix. First known use: 15th century.

Middle English *Epiphanie,* borrowed from Anglo-French *Epiphane, Epiphanie,* borrowed from Late Latin *epiphanīa, epiphania* "appearance, manifestation, Christ's first manifestation (to the Gentiles in Western tradition)," borrowed from Late Greek *epipháneia* "appearance, manifestation (of God in the Old Testament, of Christ's first coming or of the Second Coming)," going back to Greek, "appearance, coming into view, manifestation (of a deity to a worshipper), Christ's coming (in the New Testament), visible surface, outward show, fame," noun derivative of *epiphanḗs* "coming into view, appearing, manifest, evident," adjective derivative from the stem of *epiphaínein* "to show, display," mediopassive *epiphaínesthai* "to come into view, be manifested, appear on the surface," from *epi-* epi- + *phaínein* "to bring to light, cause to appear," *phaínesthai* "to become visible, appear". First known use: 14th century.
examples: … the experience is an **epiphany** whereby the true essence of cooking is revealed. — John Mariani

words.definition: Written in the form of letters
examples: … an endless sequence of … **epistolary** love affairs.

words.definition: A descriptive word or phrase attached to a name
words.origin: Latin *epitheton*, from Greek, from neuter of *epithetos* added, from *epitithenai* to put on, add, from *epi-* + *tithenai* to put. First known use: 1579.

words.definition: Calmness and composure, especially under strain
words.origin: Latin *aequanimitas*, from *aequo animo* with even mind. First known use: 1663.

words.definition: To speak ambiguously to avoid commitment

words.origin: Erst + *while* "at one time, formerly," going back to Middle English, going back to Old English *hwīle,* accusative of *hwīl* while. First known use: 1569.
examples: … cultures, **erstwhile** unknown to each other … — Robert Plank

words.origin: Middle English *erudit*, from Latin *eruditus*, from past participle of *erudire* to instruct, from *e-* + *rudis* rude, ignorant. First known use: 15th century.
examples: There was the **erudite**-but-humble professor next door and upstairs. — Maria Shine Stewart
In the telling of a life lived through books, and in her own sometimes floridly **erudite** sentences, the deep magic of writing is revealed. — Nina Renata Aron

words.definition: Understood only by a small group
words.origin: Late Latin *esotericus*, from Greek *esōterikos*, from *esōterō*, comparative of *eisō, esō* within, from *eis* into; akin to Greek *en* in. First known use: circa 1660.
examples: … a body of **esoteric** legal doctrine … — Benjamin N. Cardozo
The titles of some concert tours can be a bit **esoteric**. — Matt Wake
… the rise of a peaking full moon, which bathed the wild shore in an **ethereal** glow. — Simon Peter Groebner
… a wood thrush sang its **ethereal** song. — Taylor Piephoff

words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *euphōnia,* borrowed from Greek *euphōnía* "good voice quality (of a public speaker), good tone (of horns)," from *eúphōnos* "pleasant-sounding, musical" (from *eu-* eu- + *-phōnos* "having a sound [of the kind specified]," adjective derivative of *phōnḗ* "sound made by something living, voice, speech") + *-ia* -ia. First known use: 1606.

words.definition: Quickly fading from sight or memory
words.origin: Latin *evanescent-, evanescens*, present participle of *evanescere*. First known use: 1717.
Medieval Latin *exculpatus*, past participle of *exculpare*, from Latin *ex-* + *culpa* blame. First known use: circa 1656.
From *execrate* + *-able*. *Execrate*: Latin *exsecratus*, past participle of *exsecrari* to put under a curse, from *ex* + *sacr-, sacer* sacred. First known use: 14th century.

Borrowed from Late Latin *exēgēsis,* borrowed from Greek *exḗgēsis* "detailed account, description, exposition," from *exēgē-,* variant stem of *exēgéomai, exēgeîsthai* "to lead forth, direct, prescribe, order, dictate, expound, explain, relate" (from *ex-* ex-:3 + *hēgeîsthai* "to lead, act as guide, rule, consider, believe") + *-sis* -sis. First known use: 1627.
examples: As an **exegesis**, though, it's nicely done, and Kennedy traces Sontag's main themes deftly along tortuous paths through both essays and fiction. — Larissa MacFarquhar

words.origin: Latin *exigent-, exigens*, present participle of *exigere* to demand. First known use: 1624.

words.definition: To atone for guilt or sin
words.origin: Latin *expiatus*, past participle of *expiare* to atone for, from *ex-* + *piare* to atone for, appease, from *pius* faithful, pious. First known use: circa 1500.
examples: … permission to **expiate** their offences by their assiduous labours … — Francis Bacon

words.origin: Latin *expungere* to mark for deletion by dots, from *ex-* + *pungere* to prick. First known use: 1602.

Late Latin *extemporāneus* "done on the spur of the moment" (from Latin *ex tempore* "on the spur of the moment, extempore" + *-āneus,* suffix forming adjectives from temporal adverbs) + -ous. First known use: 1673.
examples: A great deal of criminal and delinquent behaviour is … **extemporaneous**. — W. C. Reckless

words.origin: Latin *exstirpatus*, past participle of *exstirpare*, from *ex-* + *stirp-, stirps* trunk, root. First known use: 1538.

words.definition: Treating serious matters with flippant humour
words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French *facetieux, facecieux,* from *facetie* "joke, jesting remark" (borrowed from Latin *facētia, facētiae* "cleverness, wit," in plural sense, "amusing things, jests") + *-eux* (going back to Latin *-ōsus* -ous). First known use: 1594.
examples: … a … possibly **facetious** suggestion that Texas should secede if Washington doesn't ease off … — Todd J. Gillman

words.definition: An employee who does all kinds of work
words.origin: From the Latin phrase *fac tōtum* "do all!", from *fac* (singular imperative of *facere* "to make, do" + *tōtum* "the whole, entirety," from neuter of *tōtus* "all, the whole of"). First known use: 1562.
From *fallacy* + *-ous*. *Fallacy*: Latin *fallacia*, from *fallac-, fallax* deceitful, from *fallere* to deceive. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Very attentive to accuracy and detail; fussy
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *fastidiosus*, from *fastidium* disgust, probably from *fastus* arrogance (probably akin to Latin *fastigium* top) + *taedium* irksomeness. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … regulators are guaranteed to take a **fastidious** approach in evaluating safety … — Alex Carchidi
… he took **fastidious** care of his cars. — Marga Lincoln

words.origin: Latin *fatuus* foolish. First known use: 1633.
examples: A **fatuous** socialite with a near-pathological love of parties and shopping — Janet Maslin

words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *fecundus*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Lacking initiative or strength of character
words.origin: From Scots, earlier *fectles* "valueless, futile," from *fek, fect* (later *feck*) "value, efficacy" (aphetic form of *effect* effect) + *-les* -less. First known use: circa 1585.
examples: She can't rely on her **feckless** son.
… a **feckless** maneuver that could only serve to strengthen the enemy … — Simon Schama

words.origin: From *felicity* + *-ous*. *Felicity*: Middle English *felicite*, from Anglo-French *felicité*, from Latin *felicitat-, felicitas*, from *felic-, felix* fruitful, happy. First known use: 1789.
examples: Handled the delicate matter in a most **felicitous** manner
The ride through the countryside is a **felicitous** journey for city people.

words.origin: Latin *fervidus*, from *fervēre*. First known use: 1599.
Middle English, from Latin *foetidus*, from *foetēre* to stink. First known use: 15th century.
Middle English *feter*, from Old English; akin to Old English *fōt* foot. First known use: before 12th century.
Latin, let it be done, 3rd singular present subjunctive of *fieri* to become, be done. First known use: circa 1631.
examples: According to the Bible, the world was created by **fiat**.

words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *flagrant-, flagrans* "flaming, fiery, (of a person) burning with desire, passionate," present participle of *flagrāre* "to be ablaze, burn, shine, burn (with passion, zeal)," probably derivative of an adjective **flagro-* "burning," going back to Indo-European **bhl̥g-ro-,* adjective derivative from the verbal base *bhleg-* "shine, be bright"; (sense 1) after in flagrante delicto and parallel Latin phrases. First known use: 1513.

Borrowed from Latin *flōridus* "abounding in flowers, brightly coloured, in the bloom of youth, highly coloured (of rhetoric)," adjective derivative, with the suffix *-idus,* corresponding to *flōrēre* "to bloom". First known use: 1651.
Obsolete French (now *faible*), from obsolete *foible* weak, from Old French *feble* feeble. First known use: circa 1648.
examples: … talent is always balanced by **foible**. — Janna Malamud Smith

words.definition: To stir up trouble or rebellion
words.origin: Middle English, to apply a warm substance to, from Late Latin *fomentare*, from Latin *fomentum* compress, from *fovēre* to heat, soothe; akin to Lithuanian *degti* to burn, Sanskrit *dahati* it burns. First known use: circa 1613.
From *forbear* + *-ance*. *Forbear*: Middle English *forberen*, from Old English *forberan* to endure, do without, from *for-* + *beran* to bear. First known use: 1570.
examples: The policy provides a means of **forbearance** for borrowers meeting certain criteria.
… a sudden formality in his manner, which showed that his **forbearance** was at last failing him. — Wilkie Collins

words.definition: Worn out from too much work
words.origin: Middle English *forswonke*, from Old English *forswuncen*, past participle of *forswincan* "to toil hard," from *for-* (intensive) + *swincan* "to toil".
Latin *fortuitus*; akin to Latin *fort-, fors* chance. First known use: 1653.
examples: … from a cost standpoint, the company's timing is **fortuitous**.
… belted down the stairs, and there was a **fortuitous** train. — Doris Lessing

words.origin: Fract(ion) (in sense "rupture, discord, breach of the peace") + -ious (after captious, factious). First known use: 1714.
Middle English, turned away, froward, from *fro* from + *-ward* -ward. First known use: 13th century.
Latin *fugac-, fugax*, from *fugere*. First known use: 1635.

Middle English *fulminaten* "to direct (condemnation at an offender)," borrowed from Late Latin *fulminātus,* past participle of *fulmināre* "to strike down, confound (an opponent)" (Medieval Latin, "to thunder [threats, denunciations]"), going back to Latin, "to strike (of lightning), strike like lightning," derivative of *fulmin-, fulmen* "lightning," from *fulg-* (base of *fulgēre* "to shine brightly, flash, lighten") + *-min-, -men,* resultative noun suffix. First known use: 15th century.
Middle English *fulsom, foulsome* "abundant, well-fed, plump, arousing disgust," from *ful, foul* full + *-som, -some* -some. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … describes in **fulsome** detail … — G. N. Shuster
**Fulsome** bird life. The feeder overcrowded — Maxine Kumin

words.origin: French or Latin; French *furtif*, from Latin *furtivus*, from *furtum* theft, from *fur* thief, from or akin to Greek *phōr* thief; akin to Greek *pherein* to carry. First known use: 1612.
Middle English, from Anglo-French *fustian, fustayn*, from Medieval Latin *fustaneum*, probably from *fustis* tree trunk, from Latin, stick, cudgel. First known use: 13th century.

Middle English *yein seyen, gein-seyen* "to speak in opposition to, deny," from *yein-, gein-* "away, back, against, in opposition to" (going back to Old English *gēan-* "in opposition to," or marking returning or reciprocal action, going back to Germanic **gagna-*) + *seyen* "to say". First known use: 14th century.
examples: Did not dare to **gainsay** the king

words.definition: An opening move made to gain an advantage
words.origin: Borrowed from Spanish *gambito*, borrowed from Italian *gambetto*, literally, "act of tripping someone," from *gamba* "leg" (going back to Late Latin) + *-etto*, diminutive suffix. First known use: 1656.

Borrowed from Latin *garrulus,* from *garrīre* "to chatter, talk rapidly" (probably of imitative origin) + *-ulus,* deverbal suffix denoting inclination or repetitive action (going back to Indo-European *-l-,* participial suffix). First known use: circa 1611.
French, literally, left. First known use: 1751.
examples: It would be **gauche** to mention the subject

words.origin: Middle English *germain*, literally, having the same parents, from Anglo-French. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Omit details that are not **germane** to the discussion

words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: circa 1529.
Perhaps from Middle French *giber* to shake, handle roughly. First known use: 1567.
examples: Boxers **gibing** each other before a fight

words.origin: Probably modification of Low German *glibberig* slippery. First known use: 1584.
examples: Their **glib** assurances that "everything will be fine"

words.origin: Middle English (Scots) *gloming*, from Old English *glōming*, from *glōm* twilight; akin to Old English *glōwan* to glow. First known use: before 12th century.
Middle English *gossomer*, from *gos* goose + *somer* summer. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … the **gossamer** of youth's dreams … — Andrea Parke

words.origin: Probably from Middle French, from Latin *grandiloquus* using lofty language, from *grandis* + *loqui* to speak. First known use: 1589.
Latin *gregarius* of a flock or herd, from *greg-, grex* flock, herd. First known use: 1668.
Middle English *gile*, from Anglo-French, probably of Germanic origin; akin to Old English *wigle* divination. First known use: 13th century.
examples: A war that called for **guile** rather than firepower

words.definition: Relating to the sense of taste
Idyllically happy and peaceful, as in times past
examples: **Classics Illustrated** have become pricey nostalgia items for those who grew up in the supposedly **halcyon** years after World War II. — Donna Richardson

words.origin: Middle English *happelesse,* from *happe* "luck, fortune, hap" + *-lesse* -less. First known use: 14th century.
examples: **Hapless** beings caught in the grip of forces we can do little about — W. H. Whyte

words.origin: Middle French *arenge*, from Old Italian *aringa*, from *aringare* to speak in public, from *aringo* public assembly, of Germanic origin; akin to Old High German *hring* ring. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … listening to his capacious **harangue** and its immaculate delivery … — Sir Winston Churchill
… emotional and frequently violent **harangues** … — K. E. Read

words.definition: A sign of what is to come
words.origin: Middle English *herbergere, herberjour, herbeger, harbenyowre* "member of a noble or royal retinue who assigns lodgings to guests or rides ahead to prepare an encampment, host, innkeeper," borrowed from Anglo-French *herberger, herberjur* (continental Old French *herbergeor*), from *herberger* "to lodge, shelter, encamp" (continental Old French *herbergier,* borrowed from Old Low Franconian **haribergōn,* going back to Germanic **haribergōjan-* "to set up quarters for an army") + *-er, -eor* -er. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Robins, crocuses, and other **harbingers** of spring
… I suspect the mural is a **harbinger** of things to come, that new printing techniques will usher in a revival of architectural ornament. — Karrie Jacobs

words.origin: French, from *haut* high. First known use: circa 1628.
examples: … he distances himself with customary **hauteur** from the world … — Martin Amis

words.definition: To talk to in a bullying way
words.origin: Latin, from Greek *Hektōr*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Dominance of one group over others
words.origin: Greek *hēgemonia*, from *hēgemōn* leader, from *hēgeisthai* to lead. First known use: 1567.
examples: The rise of Health Management Organizations (HMOs) and managed care in general has weakened physician **hegemony** over medicine. — Amy Agigian

words.definition: Not conforming to accepted standards or beliefs
words.origin: Late Latin *heterodoxus*, from Greek *heterodoxos*, from *heter-* + *doxa* opinion. First known use: circa 1650.

words.definition: A pause or gap in a sequence
words.origin: Latin, from *hiare* to yawn. First known use: 1563.
examples: The … weedy **hiatus** between the town and the railroad. — Willa Cather
… the **hiatus** between the theory and the practice of the party … — J. G. Colton

words.definition: Unwilling to change because of convention

words.origin: Latin *hirsutus*; akin to Latin *horrēre* to bristle. First known use: 1621.
Late Latin *histrionicus*, from Latin *histrion-, histrio* actor. First known use: 1648.

Middle English *omelie*, from Anglo-French, from Late Latin *homilia*, from Late Greek, from Greek, conversation, discourse, from *homilein* to consort with, address, from *homilos* crowd, assembly; akin to Greek *homos* same. First known use: 14th century.
Borrowed from Greek *hýbris* "arrogance, abuse, violence, outrage," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1884.
examples: Shocked by the sheer **hubris** of their comments/actions
Their story … depicts a team that became the victim of its own **hubris**.

words.origin: Latin, from Greek *hyperbolē* excess, hyperbole, hyperbola, from *hyperballein* to exceed, from *hyper-* + *ballein* to throw. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Often, referring to an athlete as an icon is an act of obvious **hyperbole**. — Chad Finn
… the show is famous for constantly using **hyperboles** like “the most shocking season” or “jaw-dropping” … — Shivani Gonzalez

words.definition: One who attacks cherished beliefs or institutions
words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *īconoclastēs* "person who destroys religious images," borrowed from Middle Greek *eikonoklástēs,* from Greek *eikono-* icono- + *-klastēs,* derivative, with the agent suffix *-tēs,* from the base of *kláō, klân* "to break off, break in pieces". First known use: 1641.

words.definition: A peculiar habit or way of behaving
words.origin: Greek *idiosynkrasia*, from *idio-* + *synkerannynai* to blend, from *syn-* + *kerannynai* to mingle, mix. First known use: 1604.
examples: When you know someone a long time, you become accustomed to their **idiosyncrasies**, which is a fancy word for their unique habits. — Lemony Snicket (Daniel Handler)
GE executives examine each country's **idiosyncrasies** microscopically, then tailor a mix of products … and retail approaches to wring the best performance from each. — Linda Grant

words.definition: An extremely happy, peaceful or picturesque scene
words.origin: Latin *idyllium*, from Greek *eidyllion*, from diminutive of *eidos* form; akin to Greek *idein* to see. First known use: 1586.
Middle French or Latin; Middle French *ignominie*, from Latin *ignominia*, from *ig-* (as in *ignorare* to be ignorant of, ignore) + *nomin-, nomen* name, repute. First known use: circa 1527.
examples: Suffered the **ignominy** of another losing season

words.origin: Italian, from *imbrogliare* to entangle, from Middle French *embrouiller*. First known use: 1750.
examples: America's president and scientific establishment became furiously embroiled with a few writers of popular nature books for children. The **imbroglio** ended in the rout of the nature writers … — Matt Cartmill

words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *immutabilis*, from *in-* + *mutabilis* mutable. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A situation in which no progress is possible
words.origin: French, from *in-* + *passer* to pass. First known use: 1851.
examples: An impossible **impasse** in which accepting a pardon meant admitting guilt

words.origin: In-:1 + obsolete English *pecunious* rich, from Middle English, from Latin *pecuniosus*, from *pecunia* money. First known use: 1596.

Borrowed from Latin *imperiōsus* "exercising authority, domineering," from *imperium* "authority over family members and slaves exercised by the head of a household, supreme administrative authority, dominion" + *-ōsus* -ous. First known use: 1529.
examples: … a kind of arrogant potentate too **imperious** to acknowledge weaknesses common to ordinary men. — Robert Dalleck
… the **imperious** problems of the new age. — John F. Kennedy

words.origin: Latin *impervius*, from *in-* + *pervius* pervious. First known use: 1615.
Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Late Latin *impetuosus*, from Latin *impetus*. First known use: 14th century.
Middle English, from Latin *implacabilis*, from *in-* + *placabilis* placable. First known use: 15th century.

Borrowed from Middle French & Medieval Latin; Middle French *importuner* "to tire, annoy by inappropriate persistence," borrowed from Medieval Latin *importūnāre* "to harass, pester," verbal derivative of Latin *importūnus* "unfavorable, inconvenient, adverse, troublesome, relentless". First known use: 1530.
examples: … he was **importuned** relentlessly by the hostess to bestow … a name. — Geoffrey Wolff

words.origin: From *imprecate* + *-ion*. *Imprecate*: Latin *imprecatus*, past participle of *imprecari*, from *in-* + *precari* to pray. First known use: 15th century.
Middle English, from Latin *impudent-, impudens*, from *in-* + *pudent-, pudens*, present participle of *pudēre* to feel shame. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Lisa is often out of the house and in motion … contending with **impudent** youths … — Robert Lloyd
When I refused to be the child they knew and accepted me to be, I was called **impudent** and my muteness sullenness. — Maya Angelou

words.definition: To dispute the truth or honesty of
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *empugner*, from Latin *inpugnare*, from *in-* + *pugnare* to fight. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Just begun and not fully formed
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *incohātus, inchoātus* "only begun, unfinished, imperfect," from past participle of *incohāre* "to start work on, begin, initiate," perhaps, if the original sense was "to yoke a plow to a team of oxen," from *in-* in-:2 + *-cohāre,* verbal derivative of *cohum* "hollow in the middle of a yoke into which a pole is fitted" or "strap used to attach the pole to the yoke," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1534.
examples: … misty, **inchoate** suspicions that all is not well with the nation … — J. M. Perry
Until an employee has earned his retirement pay … his retirement pay is but an **inchoate** right …

words.definition: In an initial stage; beginning to happen
words.origin: Latin *incipient-, incipiens*, present participle of *incipere* to begin. First known use: 1633.

words.definition: Not able to be corrected or reformed
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *incorrigibilis*, from Latin *in-* + *corrigere* to correct. First known use: 14th century.
Middle French, from Latin *indefatigabilis*, from *in-* + *defatigare* to fatigue, from *de-* + *fatigare* to fatigue. First known use: 1608.
Late Latin *indolent-, indolens* insensitive to pain, from Latin *in-* + *dolent-, dolens*, present participle of *dolēre* to feel pain. First known use: 1663.

words.definition: Too great to be expressed in words
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *ineffabilis*, from *in-* + *effabilis* capable of being expressed, from *effari* to speak out, from *ex-* + *fari* to speak. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Unable to be resisted or avoided
words.origin: Latin *ineluctabilis*, from *in-* + *eluctari* to struggle clear of, from *ex-* + *luctari* to struggle, wrestle; akin to Latin *luxus* dislocated. First known use: circa 1623.
Latin *inexorabilis*, from *in-* + *exorabilis* pliant, from *exorare* to prevail upon, from *ex-* + *orare* to speak. First known use: 1542.
Latin *ingenuus* native, freeborn, from *in-* + *gignere* to beget. First known use: 1588.
examples: … her **ingenuous** thirst for experience … — Christopher Rawson

words.definition: A cosy space beside a large fireplace
Tending to obstruct or harm; hostile
words.origin: Late Latin *inimicalis*, from Latin *inimicus* enemy. First known use: 1573.
Middle English *iniquite*, from Anglo-French *iniquité*, from Latin *iniquitat-, iniquitas*, from *iniquus* uneven, from *in-* + *aequus* equal. First known use: 14th century.
Latin *innocuus*, from *in-* + *nocēre*. First known use: 1631.
examples: … newly aware that the behaviour isn't as **innocuous** as they imagined. — Conor Friedersdorf

words.definition: Proceeding in a subtle way, but with harmful effects
words.origin: Latin *insidiosus*, from *insidiae* ambush, from *insidēre* to sit in, sit on, from *in-* + *sedēre* to sit. First known use: 1545.
French & Late Latin; French *insipide*, from Late Latin *insipidus*, from Latin *in-* + *sapidus* savory, from *sapere* to taste. First known use: 1609.
French, from *in-* + *soucier* to trouble, disturb, from Old French, from Latin *sollicitare*. First known use: 1799.
Spanish *intransigente*, from *in-* + *transigente*, present participle of *transigir* to compromise, from Latin *transigere* to come to an agreement. First known use: circa 1879.
Middle English *enuren*, from *in ure* customary, from *putten in ure* to use, put into practice, partial translation of Anglo-French *mettre en ovre, en uevre*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Policies that **inure** to the benefit of employees

words.origin: Middle English *invectif*, from Middle French, from Latin *invectivus*, from *invectus*, past participle of *invehere*. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To persuade by deception or flattery
words.origin: Anglo-French *enveegler, aveogler, avogler* to blind, hoodwink, from *avogle, enveugle* blind, from Medieval Latin *ab oculis*, literally, lacking eyes. First known use: 1539.
Middle English, from Latin *inveteratus*, from past participle of *inveterare* to age (transitive verb), from *in-* + *veter-, vetus* old. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The **inveterate** tendency to overlook the obvious

words.origin: Middle French, from Late Latin *irascibilis*, from Latin *irasci* to become angry, be angry, from *ira*. First known use: circa 1530.
Late Latin *itinerant-, itinerans*, present participle of *itinerari* to journey, from Latin *itiner-, iter* journey, way; akin to Hittite *itar* way, Latin *ire* to go. First known use: circa 1576.
Latin *jejunus* empty of food, hungry, meagre. First known use: 1646.
examples: … the "literary" fiction being written in this country nowadays strikes me as so **jejune**, self-absorbed and lifeless that I am just about unable to read it, much less pass fair judgment on it. — Jonathan Yardley

words.origin: Derivative of jettison. First known use: 1848.
examples: … must be prepared to **jettison** many romantic notions … — Christopher Catling

words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *jocōsus* "fond of jokes, given to joking, laughable," from *jocus* "joke, jest" + *-ōsus* -ose. First known use: 1673.
Middle English, from Late Latin *jocundus*, alteration of Latin *jucundus*, from *juvare* to help. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … a poet could not but be gay, in such a **jocund** company … — William Wordsworth

words.definition: To place side by side for contrast
words.origin: Probably back-formation from *juxtaposition*. First known use: 1851.
examples: … **juxtapose** unexpected combinations of colours, shapes and ideas … — J. F. T. Bugental

words.definition: Intricate and confusing, like a maze
words.origin: From *labyrinth* + *-ine*. *Labyrinth*: Middle English *laborintus*, from Latin *labyrinthus*, from Greek *labyrinthos*. First known use: 1632.
Latin *lacrimosus*, from *lacrima* "tear". First known use: circa 1727.
examples: Tended to become **lachrymose** when he was drunk

words.origin: Latin *laconicus* Spartan, from Greek *lakōnikos*; from the Spartan reputation for terseness of speech. First known use: 1589.
Latin *lambent-, lambens*, present participle of *lambere* to lick. First known use: 1647.

Borrowed from 17th-century French *lampon,* perhaps from *lampons!* "let us drink up!", first plural imperative of *lamper* "to drink up, drink to the bottom quickly," nasalized variant of *laper* "to lap, lap up," going back to Vulgar Latin **lappāre,* of expressive origin; allegedly from the use of *lampons!* in the refrains of verse satires. First known use: 1645.
examples: He said such ridiculous things that he was often the target of **lampoons** in the press.

words.origin: Middle French *languide*, from Latin *languidus*, from *languēre* to languish. First known use: 1595.
