examples: … arms too **languid** with happiness to embrace him … — John Galsworthy

words.origin: Middle English *largesse*, from Anglo-French, from *large*. First known use: 13th century.
examples: Projects depending on a flow of federal **largesse**

words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *lassitudo*, from *lassus* weary; probably akin to Old English *læt* late. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The patient complained of headache, nausea, and **lassitude**.
… surrendering to an overpowering **lassitude**, an extreme desire to sit and dream. — Alan Moorehead

words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French *leger de main* light of hand. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The … performer devised a show that attached orchestral music to her feats of **legerdemain**. — Steven Brown
… a remarkable piece of diplomatic **legerdemain** … — Anthony West

words.definition: Humour or frivolity, especially when out of place
words.origin: Latin *levitat-, levitas*, from *levis* light in weight. First known use: 1564.
examples: She would tolerate no **levity** in the classroom.
… the **levity** … of the brisk fire. — Charles Dickens

words.definition: A person who freely indulges in sensual pleasures
words.origin: Middle English, "freedman," borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *libertin,* borrowed from Latin *lībertīnus,* noun derivative from *lībertīnus,* adjective, "of a freedman," from *lībertus* "freedman" (probably back-formation from *lībertās* "freedom, liberty") + *-īnus* -ine. First known use: 1577.
examples: … **libertines** indulging a variety of amorous impulses. — Mel White

words.origin: Latin *licentiosus*, from *licentia*. First known use: 1535.

words.definition: At a boundary or threshold; in between
words.origin: Latin *limin-, limen* threshold. First known use: 1875.
examples: … in the **liminal** state between life and death. — Deborah Jowitt

words.origin: French or Latin; French *limpide*, from Latin *limpidus*, perhaps from *lympha* water. First known use: 1598.
examples: … the benign effects of a **limpid** childhood …

words.origin: Alteration of *lithesome*. First known use: 1763.

words.definition: A tedious recital or repetitive series
words.origin: Middle English *letanie*, from Anglo-French & Late Latin; Anglo-French, from Late Latin *litania*, from Late Greek *litaneia*, from Greek, entreaty, from *litanos* supplicant. First known use: 13th century.
examples: … a **litany** of cheering phrases. — Herman Wouk

words.definition: Tending to talk a great deal
words.origin: Latin *loquāc-, loquāx* "talkative, verbose" (from *loquī* "to talk, speak" + *-āc-,* deverbal suffix denoting habitual or successful performance) + -ious. First known use: 1634.
examples: … not often the most **loquacious** man when it comes to talking to the media … — Bill Reiter
The moderators have largely held their ground, … cutting off **loquacious** candidates. — Eliza Collins

words.origin: Latin *lūbricus* "slippery, hard to hold, hazardous" (Late Latin also "morally weak, lascivious") + -ious. First known use: 1535.

Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *lucrum* "material gain, profit," going back to Indo-European **lh2u-tló-* "seizure, gain," from **leh2u-* "seize, capture" + **-tlo-,* noun suffix, typically of instruments; **leh2u-* also in Greek *apolaúein* "to benefit (from), have pleasure or enjoyment," *leíā,* Doric* lāíā* "plunder, spoil," Germanic **launa-* "recompense, reward" (see guerdon). First known use: 14th century.

Borrowed from Latin *lūcubrātiōn-, lūcubrātiō* "study done by lamplight," from *lūcubrāre* "to work by lamplight" + *-tiōn-, -tiō,* suffix of verbal action; *lūcubrāre* derivative of **lūcubrum* "lamp, lamplight," from *lūc-, lūx* "light" + *-brum,* variant (after stems with an *-l-*) of *-bulum,* suffix of instruments (going back to Indo-European **-dhlom*); *-u-* presumably from *-i-/-e-* by rounding before a labial. First known use: 1595.

words.definition: Looking or sounding sad and dismal
words.origin: Latin *lugubris*, from *lugēre* to mourn; akin to Greek *lygros* mournful. First known use: 1585.
examples: … dark, dramatic and **lugubrious** brooding … — V. S. Pritchett
The tour de force of **lugubrious** cliche is ten times longer than this review — Martin Amis

words.definition: Vivid in a shocking or garish way
words.origin: Latin *luridus* pale yellow, sallow. First known use: 1603.
examples: The tabloids gave all the **lurid** details of floating wreckage and dismembered bodies.
… paperbacks in the usual **lurid** covers. — T. R. Fyvel

words.origin: Middle English *machynacion,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *māchinātiōn-, māchinātiō* "making of a machine, piece of machinery, mechanism," from *māchinārī* "to invent, devise, contrive" + *-tiōn-, -tiō,* suffix of verbal action. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … backstage **machinations** and power plays that have dominated the film industry … — Peter Bogdanovich

words.definition: Generous or forgiving, especially to a rival
words.origin: Latin *magnanimus*, from *magnus* great + *animus* spirit. First known use: 1547.
examples: … a **magnanimous** and moving gesture, suitable to the spirit of the holiday. — Maurizio Valsania
He'd have been **magnanimous** in victory and gracious in defeat. — Liam Thorp

words.definition: A general feeling of unease or discomfort
words.origin: French *malaise*, from Old French, from *mal-* + *aise* comfort. First known use: 1768.
examples: An infected person will feel a general **malaise**.
… a **malaise** of cynicism and despair … — Malcolm Boyd

words.definition: The mistaken use of a word in place of a similar-sounding one
words.origin: Mrs. *Malaprop*, character noted for her misuse of words in R. B. Sheridan's comedy *The Rivals* (1775). First known use: 1826.
examples: "Jesus healing those leopards" is an example of **malapropism**.

words.origin: Middle English *malediccioun*, from Late Latin *malediction-, maledictio*, from *maledicere* to curse, from Latin, to speak evil of, from *male* badly + *dicere* to speak, say. First known use: 14th century.
examples: But I taunted him, ridiculed him, and loaded him with **maledictions** … — Sir Walter Scott

words.origin: Latin *malevolent-, malevolens*, from *male* badly + *volent-, volens*, present participle of *velle* to wish. First known use: 1509.
examples: … scheming, of both the benevolent and **malevolent** sort, designed to steer or derail the course of love. — Don Aucoin
And then there's Helen, the **malevolent** Sicilian neighbour who wishes everyone dead … — Judith Newman

words.definition: To pretend illness to avoid duty
words.origin: French *malingre* sickly. First known use: 1820.
examples: His boss suspected him of **malingering** because of his frequent absences from work.

words.origin: Jean *Martinet*, 17th century French army officer. First known use: 1737.
examples: The prison's warden was a cruel **martinet**.
A **martinet** in conducting meetings of the society, he never tolerated any sign of "levity or indecorum." — Daniel J. Boorstin

words.definition: Getting out of bed in a bad mood
words.origin: A modern coinage, not a dictionary entry: from *Matuta*, the Roman goddess of the dawn, + Greek *lypē* "grief, sorrow".
Alteration of Mary *Magdalene*; from her depiction as a weeping penitent. First known use: 1509.
examples: … a mob of **maudlin** rummies … sing hymns … — Joseph Mitchell
Would crack open another beer and become **maudlin** — Patrick Moore

words.definition: A hypocrite who makes a show of piety; originally, a worm living in the stomach or gut
words.origin: From *maw* "stomach" + *worm*. The "hypocrite" sense comes from Mawworm, a canting preacher in Isaac Bickerstaffe's play *The Hypocrite* (1769).
Middle English *mawke* maggot, probably from Old Norse *mathkr*. First known use: circa 1697.

words.definition: Sweet or musical; pleasant to hear
words.origin: Middle English *mellyfluous*, from Late Latin *mellifluus*, from Latin *mell-, mel* honey + *fluere* to flow; akin to Goth *milith* honey, Greek *melit-, meli*. First known use: 15th century.
Latin *mendac-, mendax*. First known use: 1616.
Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *mendicant-, mendicans*, present participle of *mendicare* to beg, from *mendicus* beggar. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Subject to sudden changes of mood
words.origin: From *mercury* + *-al*. *Mercury*: Latin *Mercurius*, Roman god and the planet. First known use: 14th century.
examples: … he has a **mercurial** personality, a quality that leaves him hard to predict. — Kim Marcus
… the **mercurial**, nimble-witted types, persons given to animated speech and repartee … — A. C. Partridge

words.definition: Showily attractive but of little value
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *meretrīcius* “of women who engage in sex for financial considerations” (adjective derivative of *meretrīc-, meretrīx* “woman who engages in sex acts for financial considerations,” from *mere-,* stem of *merēre* “to earn” + *-trīc-, -trīx,* feminine agent suffix) + -ous. First known use: 1626.
examples: The paradise they found was a piece of **meretricious** trash. — Carolyn See
… scholarly names to provide fig-leaves of respectability for **meretricious** but stylish books.

words.origin: New Latin, from Greek, defilement, from *miainein* to pollute. First known use: 1665.
examples: … freed from the **miasma** of poverty … — Sir Arthur Bryant

words.origin: French, from Old French, midst, from *mi* middle (from Latin *medius*) + *lieu* place, from Latin *locus*. First known use: 1854.
examples: In this diverse **milieu**, the children found their way to a new common language. — Rebecca Mead

words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *minātōrius,* from Latin *minor, minārī* "to threaten, speak or act menacingly, hold out the threat of" (verbal derivative of *minae,* plural only, "threats, menaces, portents of evil") + *-tōrius,* deverbal adjective suffix originally forming derivatives from agent nouns ending in *-tōr-, -tor*; *minae* probably, if originally "projecting points, overhang," noun derivative of the verbal base **men-* seen in *ēminēre* "to stick out, protrude," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1532.
examples: … stabbing the air with a **minatory** forefinger. — Robert B. Silvers et al.

words.origin: Greek *misanthrōpos* hating humankind, from *misein* to hate + *anthrōpos* human being. First known use: 1683.
Middle English, from Latin, neuter of *modicus* moderate, from *modus* measure. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Had only a **modicum** of mathematical skills

words.origin: Middle English *mollifien*, from Middle French *mollifier*, from Late Latin *mollificare*, from Latin *mollis* soft; akin to Greek *amaldynein* to soften, Sanskrit *mṛdu* soft, and probably to Greek *malakos* soft, *amblys* dull, Old English *meltan* to melt. First known use: 15th century.
Middle French, present participle of *mordre* to bite, from Latin *mordēre*; perhaps akin to Sanskrit *mṛdnāti* he presses, rubs. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: At the point of death; in terminal decline
words.origin: Latin *moribundus*, from *mori* to die. First known use: circa 1721.
examples: In the **moribund** patient deepening stupor and coma are the usual preludes to death. — Norman Cameron
Prune the **moribund** files from your disk forever — D. S. Janal

words.origin: Latin *morosus*, literally, capricious, from *mor-, mos* will. First known use: 1565.

words.definition: A stubborn adherence to error despite correction

words.origin: Back-formation from *munificence*, from Latin *munificentia*, from *munificus* generous, from *munus* service, gift. First known use: 1565.
Middle English, from Middle French, from Arabic *naḍhīr* opposite. First known use: 15th century.
Latin *nascent-, nascens*, present participle of *nasci* to be born. First known use: circa 1624.
Latin *nebulosus* misty, from *nebula*. First known use: 1674.
examples: … this **nebulous** thing called jazz. — Josef Woodard
… the **nebulous** region between mere suspicion and probable cause — W. R. LaFave & J. H. Israel

words.origin: Latin *nefarius*, from *nefas* crime, from *ne-* not + *fas* right, divine law; perhaps akin to Greek *themis* law, *tithenai* to place. First known use: 1567.
examples: The more **nefarious** of these supervillains hide in plain sight. — Amelia Tait
The town itself is a classic of the genre, full of scheming locals, buried secrets and **nefarious** elites trying to make a quick buck. — David Faris

words.origin: Middle English *neophite,* borrowed from Late Latin *neophytus,* borrowed from Greek *neóphytos* "newly planted" (in New Testament and patristic Greek, "newly converted, new convert"), from *neo-* neo- + *-phytos,* verbal adjective of *phýein* "to bring forth, produce". First known use: 14th century.
examples: A **neophyte** when it comes to computers
**Neophytes** fresh from graduate schools of business

words.origin: Middle English *noysome*, from *noy* annoyance, alteration of *anoi*, from Anglo-French *anui*, from *anuier* to harass, annoy. First known use: 14th century.
Latin, neuter of *noster* our, ours, from *nos* we. First known use: 1602.
examples: … is put to work at county fairs, promoting a quack **nostrum** for pain relief. — Patrick McGrath
… an audience eager to believe he had found the **nostrum** for all of society's ills. — Warren Sloat

words.origin: Latin *nugatorius*, from *nugari* to trifle, from *nugae* trifles. First known use: 1603.
examples: The law was unenforced and thus rendered **nugatory**.

words.definition: Having a strong spiritual or divine quality
words.origin: Latin *numin-, numen* numen. First known use: 1647.

Middle English, borrowed from Late Latin *obdūrātus,* going back to Latin, past participle of *obdūrāre* "to harden, be persistent, hold out," from *ob-,* perfective prefix + *dūrāre* "to harden, hold out, endure". First known use: 15th century.
examples: Remaining **obdurate** to her husband's advances — Edith Wharton

words.origin: Borrowed from Late Latin *obfuscātus, offuscātus,* past participle of *obfuscāre, offuscāre* "to obscure, darken, depreciate," from Latin *ob-,* perfective prefix + *-fuscāre,* verbal derivative of *fuscus* "dark-coloured, sombre, dark-skinned or -complected". First known use: 1536.
examples: Moisture caused minerals in the stone and brick walls to rise up and **obfuscate** the frescoes with a thin coating of white salts. — Elizabeth Helman Minchilli
… the strong performance of the few can **obfuscate** the mediocrity of the many. — Christopher Lynch

words.origin: Middle English *obloquie, obloqui,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Late Latin; Anglo-French *obloquie,* borrowed from Late Latin *obloquium,* from *obloquī* "to speak against, blame" (going back to Latin, "to break in on, interrupt," from *ob-* "against" + *loquī* "to speak") + Latin *-ium,* deverbal suffix of function or state. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Held to their convictions in the face of **obloquy**
Living out his days in the **obloquy** of one who had betrayed a solemn trust

words.definition: Excessively eager to please or obey
words.origin: Middle English, compliant, from Latin *obsequiosus*, from *obsequium* compliance, from *obsequi* to comply, from *ob-* toward + *sequi* to follow. First known use: 1602.
examples: Was always followed around by his **obsequious** minions
There are no hushed voices, white tablecloths or **obsequious** waiters. — Isabelle Kliger

words.origin: Latin *obstreperus*, from *obstrepere* to clamour against, from *ob-* against + *strepere* to make a noise. First known use: circa 1600.
Middle English, from Latin *obtusus* blunt, dull, from past participle of *obtundere* to beat against, blunt, from *ob-* against + *tundere* to beat. First known use: 15th century.
examples: He is too **obtuse** to take a hint.
It is also, unfortunately, ill-written, and at times **obtuse** and often trivial. — Shirley Hazzard

words.definition: To remove a need or difficulty
words.origin: Late Latin *obviatus*, past participle of *obviare* to meet, withstand, from Latin *obviam*. First known use: 1567.
examples: The new medical treatment **obviates** the need for surgery.

words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *odiosus*, from *odium*. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Asserting authority in an annoyingly interfering way
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *officiōsus* "ready to fulfill obligations, dutiful, attentive, (in pejorative sense) importunate," from *officium* "beneficial act in fulfillment of an obligation, duty, functions in a position, post, office" + *-ōsus* -ous. First known use: 15th century.
examples: **Officious** people who are always ready to offer unasked advice

words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French *honereus*, from Latin *onerosus*, from *oner-, onus* burden; akin to Sanskrit *anas* cart. First known use: 14th century.

Borrowed from Latin, derivative (with *-ium,* deverbal suffix of function or state) of *opprobrāre* "to bring up as a reproach," from *ob-* ob- + *-probrāre,* verbal derivative of *probrum* "reproach, insult, disgrace," probably noun derivative of **pro-fro-* "brought up against someone (as a reproach)," going back to Indo-European **pro-bhr-o,* from **pro-* "before" + **bhr-,* ablaut grade of **bher-* "carry, bring". First known use: 1647.
examples: Collaborators with the enemy did not escape the **opprobrium** of the townspeople.
The bombing of the church was met with widespread **opprobrium**.

words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French, borrowed from Latin *opulentus* "abounding in resources, wealthy," from *op-, *ops* "power, ability, wealth" + *-ulentus* "having in quantity, full of" (probably dissimilated from **-o-u̯ent-os,* with Indo-European **-u̯ent-,* suffix of possession). First known use: circa 1518.

words.definition: To become rigid and unable to change
words.origin: Latin *oss-, os* + English *-ify*. First known use: 1699.
examples: … so easy for the mind to **ossify** and generous ideals to end in stale platitudes. — John Buchan

words.definition: Stated or appearing true, but not necessarily so
words.origin: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *ostensibilis* "perceptible, visible, capable of demonstration," from Latin *ostensus,* variant of *ostentus,* past participle of *ostendere* "to hold out for inspection, show, make clear by one's actions, demonstrate" (from *os-,* assimilated variant of *obs-,* variant of *ob-* "toward, facing, against" + *tendere* "to extend outward, stretch, spread out") + *-bilis* "capable (of acting) or worthy (of being acted upon)". First known use: 1771.
Ostentati(on) + -ous, after contention : contentious and like pairs. First known use: 1590.
examples: The **ostentatious** = very large and expensive summer homes of rich industrialists

words.definition: A secret dungeon reached through a trapdoor
words.origin: French, from Middle French, from *oublier* to forget, from Old French *oblier*, from Vulgar Latin **oblitare*, frequentative of Latin *oblivisci* to forget. First known use: 1777.
Portuguese *palavra* word, speech, from Late Latin *parabola* parable, speech. First known use: 1735.

words.definition: A manuscript written over an earlier, partly erased text
words.origin: Latin *palimpsestus*, from Greek *palimpsēstos* scraped again, from *palin* + *psēn* to rub, scrape; akin to Sanskrit *psāti, babhasti* he chews. First known use: 1825.
examples: Canada … is a **palimpsest**, an overlay of classes and generations. — Margaret Atwood
Too short a time to get to know the **palimpsest** of Genevan societies, let alone those of Switzerland — George Steiner

words.definition: To make less severe without curing
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *palliatus*, past participle of *palliare* to cloak, conceal, from Latin *pallium* cloak. First known use: 15th century.
Borrowed from Latin *pallidus* "pale, colourless". First known use: 1590.
examples: The movie is a **pallid** version of the classic novel.

words.origin: Borrowed from New Latin *panacēa* "universal remedy, cure-all," going back to Latin, "any of various medicinal plants," borrowed from Greek *panákeia* "name of a medicinal plant, universal remedy, (as a personified abstraction) a goddess of healing," derivative of *panakḗs* "all-healing," from *pan-* pan- + *-akēs,* adjective derivative of *ákos* (neuter s-stem) "cure, remedy, relief," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1548.
examples: The law will improve the lives of local farmers, but it is no **panacea**.

words.origin: Middle French *pennache*, from Old Italian *pennacchio*, from Late Latin *pinnaculum* small wing. First known use: 1553.
examples: The palace guard had a **panache** on his helmet.
… flashed his … smile and waved with the **panache** of a big-city mayor. — Joe Morgenstern

words.definition: A public speech or text in praise of someone
words.origin: Latin *panegyricus*, from Greek *panēgyrikos*, from *panēgyrikos* of or for a festival assembly, from *panēgyris* festival assembly, from *pan-* + *agyris* assembly; akin to Greek *ageirein* to gather. First known use: 1603.
examples: Composed a **panegyric** about Tchaikovsky for the concert program

words.origin: Middle French, from Old Italian *paragone*, literally, touchstone, from *paragonare* to test on a touchstone, from Greek *parakonan* to sharpen, from *para-* + *akonē* whetstone, from *akē* point; akin to Greek *akmē* point. First known use: circa 1548.
Tamil *paṟaiyan*, literally, drummer. First known use: 1613.
examples: … the mordant wit and unsettling insight that once made [Mark] Twain practically a **pariah** in Middle America. — Roy Reed
A nation, it seemed, had become a global **pariah** overnight. — Adam Westbrook and Kirk Semple

words.origin: Parsimony + -ous. First known use: 1598.

words.definition: A work imitating the style of another
words.origin: French, from Italian *pasticcio*. First known use: 1866.
examples: His building designs are **pastiches** based on classical forms.
The research paper was essentially a **pastiche** made up of passages from different sources.

words.origin: Middle English *paucite*, from Latin *paucitat-, paucitas*, from *paucus* little. First known use: 15th century.
Spanish *pecadillo*, diminutive of *pecado* sin, from Latin *peccatum*, from neuter of *peccatus*, past participle of *peccare*. First known use: 1591.
examples: The movie star's **peccadilloes** made tabloid headlines.

words.definition: Excessively concerned with minor details or rules
words.origin: From *pedant* + *-ic*. *Pedant*: Middle French, from Italian *pedante*. First known use: 1628.
examples: … **pedantic** grading rubrics and exams … — C. Brandon Ogbunu
… if we're going to be exactingly correct and **pedantic**, I'd point out that there's no such thing … — Alasdair Wilkins

words.origin: Latin *pellucidus*, from *per* through + *lucidus* lucid. First known use: 1563.

Borrowed from French, noun derivative from present participle of *pencher* "to lean, slope, be inclined, tend," going back to Old French *pengier,* going back to Vulgar Latin **pendicāre,* from **pendere* "to hang" + **-icāre,* verb formative. First known use: 1672.

words.definition: A partly shaded outer region; a borderland
words.origin: New Latin, from Latin *paene* almost + *umbra* shadow. First known use: 1665.
examples: The seventeenth century lay in the **penumbra** of the middle ages … — Edward Eggleston
The **penumbra** of the Bill of Rights

words.origin: From *penury* + *-ous*. *Penury*: Middle English, from Latin *penuria, paenuria* want; perhaps akin to Latin *paene* almost. First known use: 1590.
Latin *perambulatus*, past participle of *perambulare*, from *per-* through + *ambulare* to walk. First known use: 15th century.
From *perfidy* + *-ous*. *Perfidy*: Latin *perfidia*, from *perfidus* faithless, from *per-* detrimental to + *fides* faith. First known use: circa 1538.

words.definition: Done with minimal effort or reflection
words.origin: Late Latin *perfunctorius*, from Latin *perfungi* to accomplish, get through with, from *per-* through + *fungi* to perform. First known use: 1593.

Middle French & Latin; Middle French *peripatetique*, from Latin *peripateticus*, from Greek *peripatētikos*, from *peripatein* to walk up and down, discourse while pacing (as did Aristotle), from *peri-* + *patein* to tread; akin to Sanskrit *patha* path. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Having a harmful effect, often gradually
words.origin: Middle English, "evil, wicked," "(of an illness) extremely serious, fatal," borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *perniciōsus* "destructive of health or life, ruinous, fatal," from *perniciēs* "physicial destruction, ruin, undoing" (from *per-* per- + *nec-,* base of *necāre* "to kill, destroy" —derivative of *nec-, nex* "violent death, killing"— + *-iēs,* deverbal suffix of abstract nouns) + *-ōsus* -ous. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The study highlights just how **pernicious** this metal can be, even at low levels. — Bradley Allf

words.origin: Latin *perspicac-, perspicax*, from *perspicere*. First known use: 1640.

words.definition: Holding firmly to an opinion or course of action
words.origin: Latin *pertinac-, pertinax*, from *per-* thoroughly + *tenac-, tenax* tenacious, from *tenēre*. First known use: 1583.

words.definition: The pleasant smell of rain on dry earth
words.origin: Petr(o)- + ichor. First known use: 1964.
examples: Australian scientists first documented the process of **petrichor** formation in 1964 … — Tim Logan
The intensity of the **petrichor** smell can vary with the type of soil and how heavily the rain is falling. — John Boyer

words.origin: Earlier, "immodest, impudent," borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French, "lively, impudent," borrowed from Latin *petulant-, petulans* "impudent, self-assertive, immodest," perhaps re-formation (as a present participle) of **petulus,* adjective derivative of *petere* "to make for (with hostile intent), seek to" with *-ulus,* suffix denoting repeated or prolonged action; modern senses (since the 18th century) probably by association with pet, pettish. First known use: 1755.
examples: The person most capable of running a group of obscenely wealthy, often **petulant** twentysomethings is an obscenely wealthy, **petulant** manager. — Roy S. Johnson
"What is it all about?" cried Dorian in his **petulant** way, flinging himself down on the sofa. — Oscar Wilde

words.origin: Middle English *fleumatik, flemmatik, fleugmatik,* borrowed from Anglo-French & Late Latin; Anglo-French *fleumatike,* borrowed from Late Latin *phlegmaticus* "relating to or producing the humour phlegm," borrowed from Greek *phlegmatikós* "abounding in phlegm," from *phlegmat-, phlégma* "flame, inflammation, phlegm" + *-ikos* -ic. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Relating to the adventures of a likeable rogue
words.origin: Spanish *picaresco*, from *pícaro*. First known use: 1810.
Middle French, from present participle of *piquer*. First known use: 1645.
examples: To start, we pureed cilantro, spinach and a jalapeno in a blender to form a bright, **piquant** base for cooking the rice. — Lawman Johnson
… along the way we learn such **piquant** details as the fact that the great physicist Michael Faraday knew no math to speak of. — Tracy Kidder

words.origin: From *pith* + *-y*. *Pith*: Middle English, from Old English *pitha*; akin to Middle Dutch & Middle Low German *pit* pith, pit. First known use: 1529.
Latin *placatus*, past participle of *placare*. First known use: 1678.

words.definition: A remark used too often to be interesting
words.origin: French, from *plat* flat, dull. First known use: 1762.
examples: … he seemed to breathe only for the purpose of perpetrating puns—things of so despicable a **platitude** … — Edgar Allan Poe
… monologues with a few too many **platitudes** … — Michael Musto

words.origin: Latin *plaudite* applaud, plural imperative of *plaudere* to applaud. First known use: 1600.

Borrowed from Late Latin *plēthōra, plētūra* "fullness, overabundance of a humour," borrowed from Greek *plēthṓra* (Ionic *plēthṓrē*) "fullness, crowdedness (of a marketplace at peak hour), excess of a humour or blood," from *plēth-,* base of *plḗthein* "to be full" + *-ōra, -ōrē,* probably dissimilated variant of *-ōlē,* suffix of deverbal nouns; *plḗthein* going back to Indo-European **pléh1-dh-,* extended form of the verbal base **pleh1-* "become full," with **-dh-* marking a completed state. First known use: circa 1541.
examples: … Grand Cayman offers a **plethora** of bustling restaurants, ritzy resorts and comfortable condos … — Susanne Cummings
… a world whose credibility is threatened by the meaningless **plethora** of material goods it goes on producing. — W. Roy Niblett

words.definition: Evoking a keen sense of sadness or regret
words.origin: Middle English *poynaunt*, from Anglo-French *poinant, poignant*, present participle of *poindre* to prick, sting, from Latin *pungere*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: A **poignant** story of love, courage, and sacrifice

words.definition: A strong verbal or written attack
words.origin: French *polémique*, from Middle French, from *polemique* controversial, from Greek *polemikos* warlike, hostile, from *polemos* war; perhaps akin to Greek *pelemizein* to shake, Old English eal*felo* baleful. First known use: 1626.

words.definition: A sign that something momentous will happen
words.origin: Latin *portentum*, from neuter of *portentus*, past participle of *portendere*. First known use: 1562.

words.definition: To talk at length in a foolish way
words.origin: Low German *pratelen*; akin to Middle Dutch *praten* to prate. First known use: 1532.
examples: They **prattled** on into the night about the old days.

words.definition: Having developed abilities at an unusually early age
words.origin: Latin *praecoc-, praecox* early ripening, precocious, from *prae-* + *coquere* to cook. First known use: 1650.
examples: … Einstein was a **precocious** child. — Gemma Tarlach et al.
The wisdom out of the mouth of a **precocious** 3-year-old has, from then on, been the family's motto. — Michelle Matthews

words.origin: French *prédilection*, from Medieval Latin *praediligere* to love more, prefer, from Latin *prae-* + *diligere* to love. First known use: 1742.
examples: … a wonderfully spunky heroine with a smart mouth, a bad attitude and a **predilection** for trouble. =a tendency to get into trouble

words.definition: Having knowledge of events before they happen
words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *praescientia*, from Latin *praescient-, praesciens*, present participle of *praescire* to know beforehand, from *prae-* + *scire* to know. First known use: 14th century.
Latin *praevaricatus*, past participle of *praevaricari* to act in collusion, literally, to straddle, from *prae-* + *varicare* to straddle, from *varus* bowlegged. First known use: circa 1625.
Middle English *probite*, from Latin *probitat-, probitas*, from *probus* honest. First known use: 15th century.
Latin *proclivitas*, from *proclivis* sloping, prone, from *pro-* forward + *clivus* slope. First known use: 1561.
Latin *prodigus*, from *prodigere* to drive away, squander, from *pro-, prod-* forth + *agere* to drive. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … nature has been so **prodigal** of her bounty … — H. T. Buckle

words.definition: Remarkably great in size or degree
words.origin: From *prodigy* + *-ous*. *Prodigy*: Middle English, from Latin *prodigium* omen, monster, from *pro-, prod-* + *-igium* (akin to *aio* I say). First known use: 15th century.

Latin *profligatus*, from past participle of *profligare* to strike down, from *pro-* forward, down + *-fligare* (akin to *fligere* to strike); akin to Greek *phlibein* to squeeze. First known use: 1617.
Middle English, from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *prolix*, from Latin *prolixus* extended, from *pro-* forward + *liquēre* to be fluid. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Giving a good chance of success
words.origin: Middle English *propycyous*, from Anglo-French *propicius*, from Latin *propitius*, probably from *pro-* for + *petere* to seek. First known use: 15th century.
Late Latin *prosaicus*, from Latin *prosa* prose. First known use: 1692.
Latin *proscribere* to publish, proscribe, from *pro-* before + *scribere* to write. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Able to change frequently or easily
words.origin: From *proteus* + *-an*. *Proteus*: New Latin, from Latin, Proteus. First known use: 1594.
French or Latin; French *puéril*, from Latin *puerilis*, from *puer* boy, child; akin to Sanskrit *putra* son, child and perhaps to Greek *pais* boy, child. First known use: 1527.

words.definition: Eager or quick to argue or fight
words.origin: Latin *pugnac-, pugnax*, from *pugnare* to fight. First known use: 1642.
Middle English, from Latin *pulchritudin-, pulchritudo*, from *pulchr-, pulcher* beautiful. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Showing great attention to correct behaviour
words.origin: From *punctilio* + *-ous*. *Punctilio*: Italian & Spanish; Italian *puntiglio* point of honour, scruple, from Spanish *puntillo*, from diminutive of *punto* point, from Latin *punctum*. First known use: 1617.
Late Latin *pusillanimis*, from Latin *pusillus* very small (diminutive of *pusus* boy) + *animus* spirit; perhaps akin to Latin *puer* child. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: An awkward, complex or hazardous situation

words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: circa 1530.
examples: Had no **qualms** about asking for their help
It was about an enduring secular world where people did unspeakable things, seemingly without **qualm** and without any grave consequences to themselves. — Jim Holt

words.definition: The inherent nature of a thing; a quibble
words.origin: Middle English *quidite*, from Medieval Latin *quidditat-, quidditas* essence, from Latin *quid* what, neuter of *quis* who. First known use: 14th century.
Middle English *querelose*, from Latin *querulus*, from *queri* to complain. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Fussing over trifles; wasting time on things that don't matter
words.origin: From the verb *quiddle* "to trifle, dawdle," of uncertain origin.

Borrowed from Latin *quiēscent-, quiēscens,* present participle of *quiēscere* "to repose, fall asleep, rest, be quiet," inchoative derivative of a base *quiē-,* going back to Indo-European **kwi̯eh1-* "have a rest". First known use: 1605.
Don *Quixote*. First known use: 1718.
examples: What started as an act of rather **quixotic** nostalgia has grown into one of the most sophisticated preservation efforts in the country. — Richard Todd
… the **quixotic** search for cities of gold. — Thomas Y. Canby

words.definition: Of or occurring every day; ordinary
words.origin: Middle English *cotidian*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *quotidianus, cotidianus*, from *quotidie* every day, from *quot* (as) many as + *dies* day. First known use: 14th century.
French, from Middle French, from *raconter* to tell, from Old French, from *re-* + *aconter, acompter* to tell, count. First known use: 1819.
French *raillerie*, from Middle French, from *railler* to mock. First known use: 1643.
Middle English *rancour*, from Anglo-French *rancur*, from Late Latin *rancor* rancidity, rancour, from Latin *rancēre*. First known use: 14th century.

Latin *rapāc-, rapāx* "given to seizing or catching things (as prey), carrying away, excessively grasping" (from *rapere* "to seize and carry off" + *-āc-, -āx,* deverbal suffix denoting habitual or successful performance) + -ious. First known use: 1651.
French, from *rapprocher* to bring together, from Middle French, from *re-* + *approcher* to approach, from Old French *aprochier*, from Late Latin *appropiare*. First known use: 1809.
Middle English *rarefien, rarifien*, modification of Latin *rarefacere*, from *rarus* rare + *facere* to make. First known use: 14th century.

Late Latin *recalcitrant-, recalcitrans*, present participle of *recalcitrare* to be stubbornly disobedient, from Latin, to kick back, from *re-* + *calcitrare* to kick, from *calc-, calx* heel. First known use: 1797.
examples: Unfortunately, her new student proved particularly **recalcitrant**. — Leonardo Bevilacqua
The touch switches for the heater and the air conditioner can be **recalcitrant** as well. — Rich Ceppos

words.origin: Latin *reconditus*, past participle of *recondere* to conceal, from *re-* + *condere* to store up, from *com-* + *-dere* to put. First known use: 1619.
examples: … mentioned some more or less **recondite** fact about the origin of the holiday … — Floyd Dell

words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French, from Latin *redolent-, redolens*, present participle of *redolēre* to emit a scent, from *re-, red-* + *olēre* to smell. First known use: 15th century.
Middle English *redoutable*, from Anglo-French, from *reduter* to dread, from *re-* + *duter* to doubt. First known use: 15th century.

Borrowed from Latin *refulgentia* "resplendence, brilliance," derivative of *refulgent-, refulgens,* present participle of *refulgere* "to radiate light, shine brightly, shine with reflected light," from *re-* re- + *fulgere* "to shine brightly, flash, lighten". First known use: 1634.
Alteration of *refractary*, from Latin *refractarius*, irregular from *refragari* to oppose, from *re-* + *-fragari* (as in *suffragari* to support with one's vote). First known use: 1606.
examples: After recovery they were **refractory** to infection

words.definition: To make a forcefully reproachful protest
words.origin: Medieval Latin *remonstratus*, past participle of *remonstrare* to demonstrate, from Latin *re-* + *monstrare* to show. First known use: 1615.

Middle English *replet, replete, repleet* "filled (with), filled with food or drink, sated, having an excess of humours," borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *replet* "filled," borrowed from Latin *replētus* "full (of), fully endowed (with)," from past participle of *replēre* "to make full again, replenish, restore, fill up, sate," from *re-* re- + *plēre* "to fill". First known use: 14th century.
examples: … a book **replete** with … delicious details … — William Safire

words.origin: Middle English, from Late Latin *reprobatus*, past participle of *reprobare*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: Scrooge, a curmudgeon and a **reprobate**, is able to … become a beacon of generosity, kindness and goodwill. — Emery Cummins

words.definition: To refuse to accept; to reject
words.origin: Latin *repudiatus*, past participle of *repudiare*, from *repudium* rejection of a prospective spouse, divorce, probably from *re-* + *pudēre* to shame. First known use: 1545.
examples: … unless they **repudiated** the failed policies of the past and took decisive action, the party might fracture or lose its hold on the electorate. — Walter A. McDougall
"The incident was witnessed by … the Marquess Zanipolo, who, in consequence, has already **repudiated** his unhappy bride." — Edith Wharton

words.definition: To return a favour or avenge a wrong
words.origin: *re-* + obsolete *quite* to quit, pay, from Middle English *quiten*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: His love for her was not **requited**.

words.origin: Borrowed from Middle French & Latin; Middle French *rescinder* "to reduce, cut, cancel, break (a contract)," borrowed from Latin *rescindere* "to remove or lay bare by hewing and cutting, cut or tear open, cancel, annul," from *re-* re- + *scindere* "to split, cleave, separate". First known use: 1579.
examples: "… from this day I diet him on bread and water— **rescind** his pocket-money! …" — George Meredith
… the bean counters send letters that seem to suggest they can **rescind** the patient's good health unless he pays up immediately. — Karen Stabiner

words.origin: Latin *reticent-, reticens*, present participle of *reticēre* to keep silent, from *re-* + *tacēre* to be silent. First known use: 1825.
examples: He is **reticent**, positively closemouthed about private matters … — Tom Gliatto
The room has an aspect of **reticent** dignity. — A. N. Whitehead

words.origin: French *rêverie*, from Middle French, delirium, from *resver, rever* to wander, be delirious. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: Referring to sex in an amusingly rude way
words.origin: Middle English *ribaud* person of low status, scoundrel, lecher, from Anglo-French, from Old French *riber* to be debauched, of Germanic origin; akin to Old High German *rīban* to be in heat, copulate, literally, to rub. First known use: circa 1500.
French, irregular from *rocaille* rocaille. First known use: 1830.

words.definition: Ruddy; having a healthy red colour
words.origin: Middle English *rubicunde*, from Latin *rubicundus*, from *rubēre* to be red; akin to Latin *rubeus*. First known use: 15th century.
Latin *ruminatus*, past participle of *ruminari* to chew the cud, muse upon, from *rumin-, rumen* rumen; perhaps akin to Sanskrit *romantha* act of chewing the cud. First known use: 1533.
examples: … **ruminating** the contents of that last batch of letters … — Aldous Huxley

words.origin: French, from Old French, roundabout path taken by fleeing game, trickery, from *reuser*. First known use: 1581.

words.definition: Too important to be interfered with
words.origin: Latin *sacrosanctus*, probably from *sacro sanctus* hallowed by a sacred rite. First known use: 1601.
Latin *sagac-, sagax*, from *sagire* to perceive keenly; akin to Latin *sagus* prophetic. First known use: 1607.
examples: The judge was fair and **sagacious**. — Keith C. Burris
… the standard post-election postmortem, in which the winner is praised for his **sagacious** grasp of the hopes and anxieties of the public … — Hendrik Hertzberg

words.definition: Having undue interest in sexual matters
words.origin: Latin *salac-, salax*, from *salire* to move spasmodically, leap. First known use: circa 1645.
examples: … have fiercely denounced the book's sketches of melodramatic lovers and **salacious** partygoers … — Casey Greenfield

words.origin: Latin *salient-, saliens*, present participle of *salire* to leap. First known use: 1646.
examples: One of the **salient** features of these Celtic structures … is the extreme narrowness of the buildings in proportion to their length. — Farley Mowat
For commuters in suburban communities … safety on the city's public transportation network is a uniquely **salient** topic. — Tim Balk

words.origin: Latin *salubris*; akin to *salvus* safe, healthy. First known use: 1547.

words.definition: Optimistic, especially in a bad situation
words.origin: Middle English *sanguin*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *sanguineus*, from *sanguin-, sanguis*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Some of us hear the term AI and picture a dystopian future. … Others are more **sanguine** about our ability to control and harness technology to achieve more and greater things. — Georgene Huang
The trustees chose to take a **sanguine** approach to the future. — Michael Hiltzik

words.origin: Re-formation, with the suffix -ic, of earlier *sardonian,* from Greek *sardónios,* alteration (after *Sardónios* "Sardinian") of earlier *sardánios* "(of laughter or smiling) bitter, scornful" (of obscure origin) + -an. First known use: 1638.
examples: A **sardonic** little jab that made her visitor quiet and subdued for the rest of the night
"The Great War," used interchangeably with "the First World War" (so named in 1918 by a **sardonic** English journalist, who knew it would not be the last such conflict) … — Benjamin Schwarz

words.origin: Latin *satiatus*, past participle of *satiare*, from *satis* enough. First known use: 15th century.
Middle English, borrowed from Medieval Latin *sāturnīnus* (Latin *Sāturnīnus,* a Roman cognomen), from Latin *Sāturnus* saturn + *-īnus* -ine. First known use: 15th century.
From Latin *scintilla*. First known use: 1661.

words.definition: Making scandalous claims to damage a reputation
examples: … **scurrilous** imposters who used a religious exterior to rob poor people … — Edwin Benson

words.origin: Latin *sedulus*, from *sedulo* sincerely, diligently, from *sed-, se* without + *dolus* guile. First known use: 1540.

Middle English, from Late Latin *sempiternalis*, from Latin *sempiternus*, from *semper* ever, always, from *sem-* one, same (akin to Old Norse *samr* same) + *per* through. First known use: 15th century.
Middle English, full of meaning, from Latin *sententiosus*, from *sententia* sentence, maxim. First known use: 1509.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin *seraphicus,* from Late Latin *seraph*im seraphim + *-icus* -ic. First known use: 1536.
examples: … the immortal / Choir of Heaven's **seraphic** host. — Luther C. Riggs
“You believe it all, I suppose?” she asked with **seraphic** gravity. — Edith Wharton

words.origin: *Serendip,* variant of *Sarandīb,* Persian and Arabic name for Sri Lanka + -ity; from its possession by the heroes of the Persian fairy tale *The Three Princes of Serendip*. First known use: 1754.
examples: … materials researchers, who now rely mostly on rules of thumb, trial-and-error and **serendipity** for developing new materials. — I. Amato
… the pleasure of wandering while lost and discovering by **serendipity** interesting new places. — Katie Davis and Howard Gardner

words.definition: Excessively willing to serve or please
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French *servil,* borrowed from Latin *servīlis* "of a slave, slavish, abject," from *servus* "slave" + *-īlis* "pertaining to or characteristic of (such persons)". First known use: 15th century.
Latin *sesquipedalis*, literally, a foot and a half long, from *sesqui-* + *ped-, pes* foot. First known use: 1656.

words.definition: A custom or phrase that distinguishes a group
words.origin: Hebrew *shibbōleth* stream; from the use of this word in Judges 12 as a test to distinguish Gileadites from Ephraimites. First known use: 1638.
examples: … the old **shibboleths** come rolling off their lips … — Joseph Epstein
… today this book publishing **shibboleth** is a myth. — L. A. Wood

words.origin: Latin *sibilant-, sibilans*, present participle of *sibilare* to hiss, whistle, of imitative origin. First known use: 1669.

words.definition: An image or imitation, often unsatisfactory
words.origin: Middle English, "image, representation," borrowed from Latin *simulācrum* "likeness, visual representation, image, statue, outward appearance of a person or thing (as in the imagination or a dream), phantom, sham appearance," from *simulāre* "to pretend, produce a fraudulent imitation of, imitate" + *-crum,* suffix of instruments (dissimilated from **-clum,* going back to **-tlom*). First known use: 15th century.
examples: … a reasonable **simulacrum** of reality … — Martin Mayer

words.definition: A paid position requiring little work
words.origin: Medieval Latin *sine cura* without cure (of souls). First known use: 1662.
Latin *sinuosus*, from *sinus*. First known use: 1578.
From French *sobriquet*. First known use: 1646.

words.definition: A grammatical mistake; a breach of etiquette
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *soloecismus,* borrowed from Greek *soloikismós,* from *solikízein* "to use language incorrectly" (from *sóloikos* "non-Greek, barbarian" —of uncertain origin— + *-izein* -ize) + *-ismos* -ism; associated by popular etymology with *Sóloi,* Athenian settlement in Cilicia whose inhabitants were alleged to have spoken poor Greek. First known use: circa 1555.
Latin *sollicitus*. First known use: 1563.
Middle English *sompnolent*, from Anglo-French, from Latin *somnolentus*, from *somnus* sleep; akin to Old English *swefn* sleep, Greek *hypnos*. First known use: 15th century.
Latin *sonorus*; akin to Latin *sonus* sound. First known use: 1611.

words.definition: Clever but false argument meant to deceive
words.origin: From *sophist* + *-ry*. *Sophist*: Latin *sophista*, from Greek *sophistēs*, literally, expert, wise man, from *sophizesthai* to become wise, deceive, from *sophos* clever, wise. First known use: 14th century.
Probably from French *soporifique*, from Latin *sopor* deep sleep; akin to Latin *somnus* sleep. First known use: 1665.
Late Latin & Latin; Late Latin *spurius* false, from Latin, of illegitimate birth, from *spurius*, noun, bastard. First known use: circa 1567.
examples: The **spurious** eminence of the pop celebrity

words.definition: Very loud and powerful, of a voice
words.origin: From *stentor* + *-ian*. *Stentor*: Latin, from Greek *Stentōr* Stentor, a Greek herald in the Trojan War noted for his loud voice. First known use: 1605.
Latin *stolidus* dull, stupid. First known use: circa 1600.

words.definition: A plan to outwit an opponent
words.origin: Italian *stratagemma*, from Latin *strategema*, from Greek *stratēgēma*, from *stratēgein* to be a general, maneuver, from *stratēgos* general, from *stratos* camp, army (akin to Latin *stratus*, past participle, spread out) + *agein* to lead. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: To make feel dull or stifled
words.origin: Late Latin *stultificare* to make foolish, from Latin *stultus* foolish; akin to Latin *stolidus* stolid. First known use: 1737.
Latin *stygius*, from Greek *stygios*, from *Styg-, Styx* Styx. First known use: 1513.

words.definition: Deceit used to achieve a goal
words.origin: Late Latin *subterfugium*, from Latin *subterfugere* to escape, evade, from *subter-* secretly (from *subter* underneath; akin to Latin *sub* under) + *fugere* to flee. First known use: 1573.

words.definition: Behaving as if superior to others
words.origin: Latin *superciliosus*, from *supercilium* eyebrow, haughtiness, from *super-* + *-cilium* eyelid (akin to *celare* to hide). First known use: 1543.
examples: Reacted to their breach of etiquette with a **supercilious** smile

words.origin: Middle English *surfet*, from Anglo-French, from *surfaire* to overdo, from *sur-* + *faire* to do, from Latin *facere*. First known use: 14th century.
Middle English, from Latin *surrepticius*, from *surreptus*, past participle of *surripere* to snatch secretly, from *sub-* + *rapere* to seize. First known use: 15th century.
Latin, hum, whisper. First known use: 1826.

words.definition: A person devoted to luxury and pleasure
A person who flatters to gain advantage
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *sȳcophanta,* borrowed from Greek *sȳkophántēs,* literally, "one who shows the fig," from *sŷkon* "fig" (perhaps in reference to an apotropaic gesture made by inserting the thumb between the index and second fingers) + *-phantēs,* agentive derivative of *phaínein* "to reveal, show, make known"; perhaps from the use of such a gesture in denouncing a culprit. First known use: 1575.
examples: … bumbling **sycophants** whose self-importance far outstrips their actual abilities. — Alison Herman

words.origin: Middle English *silogisme*, from Anglo-French *sillogisme*, from Latin *syllogismus*, from Greek *syllogismos*, from *syllogizesthai* to syllogize, from *syn-* + *logizesthai* to calculate, from *logos* reckoning, word. First known use: 14th century.
French or Latin; French *taciturne*, from Middle French, from Latin *taciturnus*, from *tacitus*. First known use: 1734.
Obsolete *tantamount*, noun, equivalent, from Anglo-French *tant amunter* to amount to as much. First known use: 1641.

words.definition: Showy but cheap and of poor quality
words.origin: *tawdry lace* a tie of lace for the neck, from *St. Audrey* (St. Etheldreda) †679 queen of Northumbria. First known use: 1655.
examples: Any trip there carries with it more than its share of drabness, **tawdry** hotels and second-rate service, all of which tax the forbearance of the most patient traveller. — John F. Burns
A **tawdry** attempt to smear his opponent

words.origin: Middle English *temeryte,* borrowed from Latin *temeritāt- temeritās,* from *temere* "blindly, recklessly, haphazardly" + *-itāt- -itās* -ity; *temere* going back to adverbialized locative singular of a noun **temes-* "darkness," going back to Indo-European **temH-es-,* whence also Sanskrit *tamas-* "darkness, gloom," Avestan *tǝmah-,* and, from the base **temH-,* Lithuanian *témsta, témti* "to become dark," *tamsà* "darkness," *tim͂sras* "dark red (of a horse), sorrel," Old Church Slavic *tĭma* "darkness," *tĭmĭnŭ* "dark, gloomy," and from a **-ro-* adjectival derivative Sanskrit *tamra-* "darkening, oppressive," Germanic **þemra-* "darkness," whence Old High German *demar* "dusk, twilight". First known use: 15th century.
Middle English *tenebrose, tenebrus,* borrowed from Anglo-French *tenebreus,* borrowed from Latin *tenebrōsus,* from *tenebrae* "darkness" + *-ōsus* -ous. First known use: 15th century.
Latin *tenuis* "fine-drawn, thin, narrow, slight" + -ous. First known use: 1597.
From Middle English *termagant*. First known use: 13th century.

words.definition: A song or poem of lament
words.origin: Greek *thrēnōidia*, from *thrēnos* dirge + *aeidein* to sing. First known use: 1634.
Middle English, from Medieval Latin *timorosus*, from Latin *timor* fear, from *timēre* to fear. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … reproached myself with being so **timorous** and cautious … — Daniel Defoe
… proceed with doubtful and **timorous** steps. — Edward Gibbon

words.origin: Latin *tintinnabulum* bell, from *tintinnare* to ring, jingle, from *tinnire*. First known use: 1831.
French, shot, tirade, from Middle French, from Old Italian *tirata*, from *tirare* to draw, shoot. First known use: 1802.

Middle English, "inattentive, lazy," borrowed from Latin *torpidus* "numbed, paralyzed," adjective derivative corresponding to the stative verb *torpēre* "to be numb, lack sensation, be struck motionless, be sluggish or lethargic," going back to dialectal Indo-European **tr̥p-eh2-* (whence also Old Church Slavic *trĭpěti* "to be patient, suffer," Lithuanian *tirpstù, tir͂pti* "to become stiff, lose feeling, fall asleep [of limbs]"), zero-grade derivative of a verbal base perhaps seen also in the Germanic adjective **þerba-* (from **terp-o-*), whence Old English *þeorf* "unleavened," Old Frisian *therve, derve* "rough, violent," Old High German *therp, derp* "unleavened," Old Icelandic *þjarfr* "unleavened, fresh (of water), insipid, flat". First known use: 15th century.
Latin *tractabilis*, from *tractare* to handle, treat. First known use: 1502.

words.definition: To transform in a surprising or magical way
words.origin: Origin unknown. First known use: 1656.
Middle English *trenchaunt*, from Anglo-French, present participle of *trencher*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: The **trenchant** divisions between right and wrong … — Edith Wharton

words.definition: A feeling of fear about what may happen
words.origin: Latin *trepidation-, trepidatio*, from *trepidare* to tremble, from *trepidus* agitated; probably akin to Old English *thrafian* to urge, push, Greek *trapein* to press grapes. First known use: 1605.
examples: Travers sent the book to press with some **trepidation**, fearing that a children's book might undermine her hard-won literary cachet. — Caitlin Flanagan

words.definition: Eager to argue or fight; defiant
words.origin: Latin *truculentus*, from *truc-, trux* savage; perhaps akin to Middle Irish *trú* doomed person. First known use: circa 1540.
examples: … he stood, hands on hips, at his most evidently **truculent** … — John Arlott

words.origin: Latin *turgidus*, from *turgēre* to be swollen. First known use: 1620.
Middle French, from Latin *turpitudo*, from *turpis* vile, base. First known use: 15th century.

Middle English, from Anglo-French, from Latin *umbraticum*, neuter of *umbraticus* of shade, from *umbratus*, past participle of *umbrare* to shade, from *umbra* shade, shadow; akin to Lithuanian *unksmė* shadow. First known use: 15th century.
examples: … the shock jock turned media power broker vacillated between contrition and **umbrage** … — Raina Kelley et al.
If someone disagrees with him, he doesn't **take umbrage**. — Fred Barnes

words.origin: Middle English, from Middle French or Medieval Latin; Middle French *unctueus*, from Medieval Latin *unctuosus*, from Latin *unctus* act of anointing, from *unguere* to anoint. First known use: 14th century.
examples: An **unctuous** appraisal of the boss's decision
… delectably **unctuous** bacon-wrapped black cod. — Caroline Bates

words.definition: To move with a smooth wavelike motion
words.origin: Latin *undulatus*, from **undula*, diminutive of *unda* wave. First known use: 1658.
Middle English *upbreyden*, from Old English *ūpbregdan*, probably from *ūp* up + *bregdan* to snatch, move suddenly. First known use: 13th century.
examples: … **upbraids** all forms of ceremony … — W. B. Yeats
**Upbraided** them for not helping their grandparents

words.origin: Latin *urbanus* urban, urbane. First known use: circa 1623.

words.definition: To take a position or power illegally
words.origin: Middle English, from Anglo-French *usorper*, from Latin *usurpare* to take possession of without legal claim, from *usu* (ablative of *usus* use) + *rapere* to seize. First known use: 14th century.
examples: **Usurped** the rights to her life story
Must not let stock responses based on inherited prejudice **usurp** careful judgment

words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *vacillātus*, past participle of *vacillāre* "to be unsteady, totter, be weak or inconstant, waver," of uncertain origin. First known use: 1597.

words.definition: Showing a lack of thought or intelligence
words.origin: Latin *vacuus* "empty, unoccupied, idle" + -ous. First known use: circa 1660.
Middle English *vaynegloryous*, from *vaynglorie* vainglory + *-ous* -ous, after Middle French *vaneglorious* and Medieval Latin *vāniglōrius*. First known use: 15th century.

Borrowed from New Latin *valedictōrius*, from Latin *valedic-*, alternate stem of *vale dīcere, valedīcere* "to say goodbye" + *-tōrius*, adjective suffix (originally derivatives of agent nouns ending in *-tōr-, -tor*). First known use: 1651.
Borrowed from Latin *vapidus* "(of wine) having lost freshness, flat"; akin to Latin *vappa* "wine that has gone flat" and perhaps to *vapor* "exhalation, steam". First known use: circa 1656.
examples: … a gossipy, **vapid** woman, obsessed by her own elegance … — R. F. Delderfield
London was not all **vapid** dissipation — V. S. Pritchett

words.definition: Marked with patches of different colours
words.origin: From past participle of variegate. First known use: 1615.

Borrowed from Middle French, going back to Old French, borrowed from Latin *vehement-, vehemens, vēmens* "violent, vigorous, (of feelings) overmastering, powerful," perhaps from *vehere* "to convey, carry along, drive" + *-mens*, adjective suffix (as in *clēmens* "mild, calm") of uncertain origin. First known use: 15th century.

Borrowed from Latin *vēnālis* "that may be bought, for sale," from **vēnus* "sale" (attested only in accusative *vēnum* and dative *vēnō, vēnuī*; akin to Greek *ônos* "price," Sanskrit *vasna-* "price, value") + *-ālis* -al. First known use: 1652.

words.definition: Respected because of age or wisdom
words.origin: Middle English, borrowed from Anglo-French & Latin; Anglo-French, borrowed from Latin *venerābilis* "entitled to respect," from *venerārī* "to solicit the good will of (a deity), hold in awe, venerate" + *-bilis* "capable of (acting or being acted upon)". First known use: 15th century.
Borrowed from Latin *verbōsus*, from *verbum* "word, verb" + *-ōsus* -ose. First known use: circa 1531.

Contracted from Middle French *verdoyant*, from present participle of *verdoyer* "to be green, turn green," going back to Old French *verdoier*, from *verd, vert* "green" (going back to Latin *viridis*, from a base **wir-*, whence *virēre* "to show green growth, be green" of uncertain origin) + *-oier*, factitive verb suffix, going back to Latin *-idiāre*, originally representing variant pronunciation (or spelling variant) of *-izāre* -ize. First known use: 1581.

words.definition: The appearance of being true or real
words.origin: Borrowed from Latin *vērīsimilitūdō*, from *vērī similis, vērīsimilis* "having the appearance of truth" + *-tūdō*, suffix of abstract nouns. First known use: circa 1576.

words.definition: The ordinary language of a region
words.origin: Latin *vernāculus* "belonging to the household, domestic, native" (from *verna* "slave born in the household"—of uncertain origin— + *-āculus*, perhaps originally diminutive suffix, though derivation is unclear) + -ar. First known use: 1601.

words.definition: Extremely high or steep; causing dizziness
words.origin: Latin *vertiginosus*, from *vertigin-, vertigo*. First known use: 1608.
Latin *vicarius*, from *vicis* change, alternation, stead. First known use: 1637.
examples: **Vicarious** menstruation manifested by bleeding from the nose

words.definition: A change of circumstances, often unwelcome
words.origin: Middle French, from Latin *vicissitudo*, from *vicissim* in turn, from *vicis* change, alternation. First known use: circa 1576.

words.definition: To speak about in an abusively disparaging way
words.origin: Middle English *vilifien*, from Late Latin *vilificare*, from Latin *vilis* cheap, vile. First known use: 15th century.

words.definition: A domineering, violent or bad-tempered woman
words.origin: Middle English, from Latin *viragin-, virago*, from *vir* man. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: Extremely severe or harmful; bitterly hostile
words.origin: Middle English, "discharging watery pus, purulent," borrowed from Latin *vīrulentus* "full of poison, venomous," from *vīrus* "venom, poisonous fluid" + *-ulentus* "having in quantity, full of". First known use: 14th century.

Middle English *viscouse*, from Anglo-French *viscos*, from Late Latin *viscosus* full of birdlime, viscous, from Latin *viscum* mistletoe, birdlime; akin to Old High German *wīhsila* cherry, Greek *ixos* mistletoe. First known use: 14th century.

Middle English, from Anglo-French *vitriole*, from Medieval Latin *vitriolum*, alteration of Late Latin *vitreolum*, neuter of *vitreolus* glassy, from Latin *vitreus* vitreous. First known use: 14th century.

words.definition: To blame or insult in strong language
words.origin: Latin *vituperatus*, past participle of *vituperare*, from *vitium* fault + *parare* to make, prepare. First known use: 1542.
Latin *vivac-, vivax* long-lived, vigorous, high-spirited, from *vivere* to live. First known use: circa 1645.
Latin *vōciferārī* "to utter with a loud voice, shout, yell" + -ous. First known use: 1700.

words.definition: The faculty of using one's will
words.origin: French, from Medieval Latin *volition-, volitio*, from Latin *vol-* (stem of *velle* to will, wish) + *-ition-, -itio* (as in Latin *position-, positio* position). First known use: 1605.

Middle English *volible, voluble* "able to turn, changing," borrowed from Latin *volūbilis* "turning on its axis, rolling, flowing, (of speech) readily flowing, fluent," from *volū-,* variant stem of *volvere* "to set in a circular course, cause to roll" + *-bilis* "capable (of acting) or worthy (of being acted upon)". First known use: 15th century.
Latin *vorac-, vorax*, from *vorare* to devour; akin to Old English ā*cweorran* to guzzle, Latin *gurges* whirlpool, Greek *bibrōskein* to devour. First known use: 1599.
From *wag* + *-ish*. *Wag*: Middle English *waggen*; akin to Middle High German *wacken* to totter, Old English *wegan* to move. First known use: 1589.

Middle English, from *wan-* deficient, wrong, mis- (from Old English, from *wan* deficient) + *towen*, past participle of *teen* to draw, train, discipline, from Old English *tēon*. First known use: 14th century.

Middle English *welteren, weltryn* "to turn over, tumble, writhe, take unrestrained pleasure (in)," frequentative derivative of *welten* "to topple, overturn, fall over," by-form (perhaps from a Germanic weak verb **waltjan-*) of *walten* "to turn over, upend, be overturned, cast, throw, surge," going back to Old English *-wæltan* (in *gewæltan* "to roll"), going back to a Germanic verbal base **walt-, *welt-* "roll," found in a variety of attested formations (as Old English *awyltan* "to roll away," *unwealt* "steady," Middle High German *walzen* "to roll over," Old Icelandic *velta* [strong verb, intransitive] "to roll, roll over," *velta* [transitive] "to set rolling," Gothic *waltjan* "to surge against [of waves]," *uswaltjan* "to overturn"), going back to Indo-European **u̯el-d-,* extended form of **u̯el(H)-* "roll," whence, with various vowel grades and stem formations, Old Irish *fillid* "(s/he) bends, turns back" (< **u̯el-n-*), Old Church Slavic *valiti sę* "to roll (intransitive)," Lithuanian *veliù, vélti* "to full (cloth), roll," Greek *eiléō, eileîn* "wind, turn round, roll up" (< **u̯el-né-*), *íllō, íllein* in same sense (< **u̯i-u̯l-ō*), Armenian *glem* "to roll". First known use: 14th century.
Irregular from *whim-wham*. First known use: 1605.
examples: The designer's new line showed a touch of **whimsy**

words.definition: In a direction contrary to the sun's course; anticlockwise
words.origin: Middle Low German *weddersinnes*, from Middle High German *widersinnes*, from *widersinnen* to go against, from *wider* back against (from Old High German *widar*) + *sinnen* to travel, go; akin to Old High German *sendan* to send. First known use: 1545.

words.definition: Having a feeling of vague, regretful longing
words.origin: Blend of *wishful* and obsolete English *wistly* intently. First known use: 1714.
Middle English *wisenen*, from Old English *wisnian*; akin to Old High German *wesanēn* to wither, Lithuanian *vysti*. First known use: before 12th century.
Middle English *wo begon*, from *wo*, noun + *begon*, past participle of *begon* to go about, beset, from Old English *begān*, from *be-* + *gān* to go. First known use: 14th century.
Origin unknown. First known use: 1513.

words.definition: A person who is fanatical in their beliefs
words.origin: Late Latin *zelotes*, from Greek *zēlōtēs*, from *zēlos*. First known use: 1537.

words.definition: The defining spirit or mood of an era
words.origin: German, from *Zeit + Geist* spirit. First known use: 1835.

Middle English *cenyth, senyth*, from Middle French *cenit*, from Medieval Latin, from Old Spanish *zenit*, modification of Arabic *samt* (*al-ra's*) way (over one's head). First known use: 14th century.
examples: … at the **zenith** of his powers … — John Buchan

words.origin: Middle English *Zephirus*, west wind (personified), from Latin *Zephyrus*, god of the west wind & *zephyrus* west wind, zephyr, from Greek *Zephyros* & *zephyros*. First known use: 1567.
